In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang

Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang , the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.

Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.

Five big stories

UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.

Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years , setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.

Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people , especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.

In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affair

Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.

US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.

Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here ). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.

The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China ? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …

Who is Alice Huang?

Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.

There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.

Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.

What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?

The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”

Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).

“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.

China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”

“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.

What approach has the US taken?

Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump . He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.

Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.

But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing him as an “honourable guy” who “built a great American company”.

Cricket | White-ball tour begins in Perth on Friday , but there is only one story in Australian cricket and the tourists are not it.

Fifa | A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.

The front pages

“TV industry must tackle abuse or face crackdown, ministers warn”, is the Guardian ’s splash today. Metro writes “Another mystery star bids to block claims”.

The Times writes “Milburn: Cut sick benefits to force young into work”, and the i Paper has “Under-25s with ADHD won’t get £217-a-month benefits in new welfare reforms”.

The FT leads with “Democrats pledge to expose ‘absolute avalanche of corruption’ under Trump”, the Mail has “Even Cameron tells PM: Don’t rejoin the EU”, and the Telegraph writes “SAS issues warning over troop witch hunts”. The Mirror says “Not even a bed for an OAP with cancer”, and the Express has “‘Sanctuary in nature helped me to recover’”.

The Latest

Trump’s $10bn BBC battle: judge rules lawsuit can go ahead

Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC has been granted permission to proceed, after the corporation’s attempt to get it dismissed was thrown out by a Trump-appointed Florida judge. The case focuses on an edit in a 2024 Panorama documentary that spliced two comments together that were made by the president during a rally before the January 6 Capitol riots, for which the BBC has apologised. With the lawsuit now set to continue, what’s at stake for press freedom? Lucy Hough speaks to global editor, Devika Bhat .

The Upside

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Researchers from the Hoag Family Cancer Institute have made a potential breakthrough in the early diagnosis of ovarian cancer – a disease often detected after it has spread.

For decades, efforts to detect the cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours. “We asked … what if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” said study leader Rajan Gogna.

Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The study found that women experiencing these changes have elevated levels of a molecule called Tu-Stroma in their blood.

The study’s co-author Dr Esha Madan says the discovery “could transform how we approach prevention”.

stories.title: Trump admin loses fight to spy on random journalists’ LinkedIn DMs
stories.summary: Confidential sources “lifeblood” of free press, court rules in LinkedIn fight.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Confidential sources “lifeblood” of free press, court rules in LinkedIn fight.

The Trump administration’s fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can’t sweep in “a vast number of confidential sources” of random journalists “who have no conceivable relationship” to the Department of Justice’s investigation, an appeals court ruled Tuesday.

The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted.

The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. So allowing that government overreach went beyond harming targeted journalists and threatened to undermine a critical platform where journalists frequently connect with confidential sources, judges ruled. Even more concerning, the Trump administration secured a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year. That left journalists unaware for far too long that their First Amendment rights had been compromised, judges ruled.

Judge: Security and free speech can coexist

Penning the unanimous opinion from a three-judge panel, Ronald Reagan-nominated judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III rejected LinkedIn’s request to quash the order entirely and ordered the US district court to substantially narrow the order to avoid posing a grave threat to press freedoms.

Without such an intervention, the US risked silencing dissidents who raise alarms about “events of large importance and governmental behavior of dubious legality and integrity,” Wilkinson wrote. “A request by the government to scoop up reporters’ records wholesale and ascertain the identity of their sources would tip the balance against informed discourse in a manner inimical to democratic health.”

“Many of the users identified have no conceivable relationship to the leak investigation,” Wilkinson wrote. “Instead, they are affiliated with media outlets, universities, and law firms which may have been relevant to the host of other stories the targeted journalists were investigating during the same considerable time period.”

As Wilkinson explained, the district court failed to consider LinkedIn’s claims that the request imposed undue burdens and threatened the First Amendment rights of users who would have no way of knowing that their communications were being reviewed by the government. The lower court reasoned that the request imposed no burden on LinkedIn because the company could feasibly respond to it, then ruled that, regardless of how these matters were weighed, the balance would tip toward the government’s interest in obtaining the LinkedIn data.

This was an error that must be corrected, the appeals court ruled.

“It is not appropriate for district courts to approve requests purely because the records requested are logistically feasible to compile,” Wilkinson wrote. He further emphasized that “serious security and speech claims are in tension in this case. There is space under law for both.”

Press advocates celebrate win

The appeals court has ordered the district court to go back and assess how the disclosure order can be narrowed. That includes entertaining a very limited alternative to the government’s secrecy order that LinkedIn had proposed—which would have notified a single attorney of the news outlet under investigation about the government’s request.

The Trump administration fought that limited request, arguing that the news outlet’s attorney may not be trustworthy or could possibly tip others off to the LinkedIn probe, but Wilkinson rejected those arguments. Noting that the justice system often deals with “imperfectly informed litigants,” Wilkinson said that “the government should be given an opportunity to explain why LinkedIn’s narrow disclosure would somehow compromise its investigation.”

“Unless the government’s response to LinkedIn’s proposal is more persuasive than anything the government has presented thus far, LinkedIn’s narrow exception to the breadth of the Secrecy Order must be adopted,” Wilkinson wrote.

LinkedIn, which is owned by Microsoft, does not seem to expect the government to be able to defend the sweeping request on remand. While a narrowed order may not protect all irrelevant users from being caught in the government’s hunt for the military leaker, it would stop Trump from accessing a broad range of journalists’ interactions with confidential sources. In a statement, a Microsoft spokesperson told Ars that “this is an important ruling for the right to privacy and press freedom.”

“Microsoft has consistently defended journalists’ ability to protect confidential sources and the principle that government demands for information should face meaningful judicial scrutiny and be balanced against First Amendment protections,” Microsoft’s spokesperson said.

Several civil rights groups backed LinkedIn in the fight, including the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP). In a statement to Ars, RCFP President Bruce D. Brown celebrated the ruling as a win for all journalists, not just those who rely on LinkedIn to connect with confidential sources.

“This ruling is a big deal and will quickly become one of the leading opinions in the area—one we will be quoting from it for a long time,” Brown said. “The court recognized that confidential sources are the ‘lifeblood’ of investigative reporting and that dragnet demands from technology companies to reveal those sources violate the law.”

stories.title: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
stories.summary: Some people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland can get help with heating costs during cold spells.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 9 February 2021

As temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments.

This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures.

In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets.

What are cold weather payments?

The cold weather payment is a government benefit top-up to help with fuel bills , external .

The average temperature in a local area must be recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven days in a row.

The temperature is recorded by the relevant weather station for your postcode.

England and Wales: Enter your postcode here to check eligibility , external

Northern Ireland: Enter your postcode here to check eligibility , external

More than 1.4 million cold weather payments were made during winter 2025-26.

Check the UK weather warnings in place

Who can get cold weather payments and how much are they worth?

To qualify, you must live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland.

Payments are not age-related but you must already be receiving certain benefits, including:

pension credit

income support

income-based job seekers' allowance

income-related employment and support allowance

universal credit - although there are certain exceptions

support for mortgage interest

Each cold weather payment is for a seven-day period and is worth £25.

More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather.

The scheme runs between 1 November and 31 March each year.

Hospital stays can affect your entitlement to the payment so you should tell the Pension Service , external or Jobcentre Plus , external if you become an inpatient.

You should also update the relevant service if you have a baby, or if a child under five comes to live with you.

In Scotland, the winter heating payment is worth £62 , external , and is paid automatically between December and February.

Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed Published 2 January

How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips Published 2 January

How to drive in snow and icy weather Published 2 January

How do cold weather health alerts work? Published 22 June

How do I get cold weather payments and how long does it take?

You do not have to do anything in order to receive cold weather payments.

The money should be paid automatically into the same bank or building society account as your benefits, within two weeks of the qualifying period of cold weather.

If you do not receive a payment, you can contact the Pension Service , external or Jobcentre Plus , external .

Cold weather payments do not affect other benefits.

They are separate to the winter fuel payment , which is worth £100 or £300 depending on your individual circumstances.

About nine million pensioners get the Winter Fuel Payment, after a government u-turn over changes to the eligibility rules.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair must be the costliest fling in human history – and a preview of what awaits when the tech bubble bursts

O ne thing we all know about the tech billionaires is they are super-smart. We know this largely because they never stop telling us. The “ cognitive elite ”, to use their favoured phrase, are entitled to shape our future without our say-so. When Elon Musk goes hiring, he wants “super-high-IQ small-government revolutionaries”. Long before they got private jets, what fuelled these boys was faith in their own brainpower. As a teenager, Jensen Huang wooed his future wife, Lori, thus: “If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you you’ll get straight As.”

Lord Byron: I believe it’s your move.

Which raises the question: if you’re that clever, why act so dumb? At last week’s midterms, it was Musk who backed Team Trump to the tune of $446m. With unhedged bets like that, why wouldn’t you want him gambling with your livelihood? This week, it is 63-year-old Huang and his affair with a much younger woman, who the US government strongly suspects is a Chinese spy. That scandal wiped more than $400bn off the value of his company in just two days, making it the costliest fling in human history. But who knows? Perhaps she loved the centibillionaire for his mind.

Forget Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: no one is more central to the future of technology than Huang. He runs Nvidia, which makes the chips powering AI. Previous generations of chips have been compared to kitchen knives: however sharp, they only chop one vegetable at a time. But the graphics-processing units made by Huang’s business are more like food blenders – they can blitz an entire veg patch. That’s what makes Nvidia the foundational infrastructure company of AI and one of the most valuable businesses in the world. And it uses its power: in some of the biggest funny-money deals over the past year in AI, Nvidia has been the money printer . It also stumped up at least $20m for Donald Trump’s new ballroom . Smart!

Not only is Huang one of Trump’s favourite businessmen, he’s warmly welcomed by leaders around the world – including Andy Burnham, who last month in London sank a whisky with him . Even as he falls from grace, Huang’s supporters have brought out the superlatives : “torchbearer”, “irreplaceable”, “incredible human”.

Huang is boss of the most strategically important business in the fastest-growing, biggest-spending industry in the world’s No 1 capitalist economy. He is part of a tiny coterie of people, who may well feel they sit above the norms and laws that govern the rest of us. That’s certainly the way he has been treated so far by Trump, who was personally warned aboard Air Force One that Huang’s love interest is believed to be a spy for Beijing. Not only is China an ever-greater threat to US AI dominance, it has been banned by Washington from getting Nvidia’s top-of-the-range chips. And the US president takes no discernible action.

Some people are in a huge tizz about the spy part of this story, notably the Tory MP Tom Tugendhat, who, after Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine , demanded that every Russian in Britain be rounded up and expelled. The force is not strong in that one. Personally, I can’t get too excited about the threat to the Trumpian model of AI. Neither, it seems, can Washington: it’s been more than a year since Nvidia was revealed to be selling some of its best stuff to a “ dilapidated storefront ” outside Kuala Lumpur, which sounded awfully like a pit stop on the way to China. Again, no action. The message ordinary Americans can take from this is that a company so vital to America’s AI-military complex is too big to subject to ordinary laws.

In the everyday world, a CEO who gets into both a sex scandal and a national-security imbroglio wouldn’t stay CEO for more than a minute. At Nvidia, the board has moved with incredible sloth. It declared on Sunday that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” – before any independent investigation. It finally met on Wednesday evening after further revelations of a separate extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang’s fate now reportedly hangs in the balance, but the company board, it may surprise you to know, includes several of his longstanding business associates . You’ll also be gobsmacked to learn that several members of his family are serving in senior positions at Nvidia.

One of the protections for Huang, like Musk and Zuckerberg and Altman, is that there appears to be no succession plan in place should any of those men fall under a self-driving automobile. A suggestion doing the rounds is that the father may now be replaced by one of his children. The Vatican has a more codified succession process for the pope, even if it includes white smoke and Ralph Fiennes .

This scandal is different from the allegations over David Walliams or the convictions handed down against Russell Brand – but one black thread that connects them is the grace afforded to each man by enablers and the powerful. Asked about the Huang affair, Trump described him as a “fine person”. Many of us will remember Trump defending the white nationalists who stormed Charlottesville in 2017. They were “some very fine people”, he said.

after newsletter promotion

This is the very same sense of impunity that drove so many Americans out last week to protest against Trump, datacentres and AI. At the midterms, the Democrats rode a wave of populism: the many v the money. Nearly two decades after the banking crash, the public anger against an unaccountable, ruinous elite is finally finding a political vehicle. Yet it still lacks the policies to match.

What do even the brightest minds in the Democratic party, or Labour for that matter, want to do about the tech billionaires? A moratorium on datacentres, certainly. A wealth tax, maybe. Given the largeness of the moment, the scale of popular anger, these are tiny measures. What about breaking up private monopolies such as Nvidia and socialising AI? How about combining that with a refoundation of welfare and other essentials of everyday life?

The tech bubble hasn’t burst, but this week we got a small taste of how it might end. When America’s AI bets do collapse, that will be a financial failure, an economic failure and a political failure. Given the strategic importance of these companies and their technologies, there will be demands for huge bailouts. The left should start preparing its own response. Through diffidence and a lack of preparation, it squandered the crisis of 2008; it mustn’t this time. To do so would not be, well, smart.

Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist

stories.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
stories.summary: The proposed radical overhaul of the welfare system would move under-25s off the main sickness benefits.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Alan Milburn will publish his review next week

Published 11 November 2026

Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

As reported in the Times, , external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment.

Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes.

People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work.

In his interim report, , external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."

Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.

Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around.

"What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC.

"Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added.

But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants.

'Cannot assume'

Tom Ashforth, a 19-year-old student at Sheffield Hallam University, receives both components of Pip at the higher rate.

He said the financial support helps him manage additional expenses linked to his visual impairment, including prescriptions, mobility aids and accessible learning resources.

"If I were to lose it, I would struggle to afford essential things," he said.

Student Tom said he relies on the money he gets from Pip to support him through his time at university

He said he believes decisions over disability benefits should be made on a case-by-case basis, rather than according to age.

"You cannot assume that everyone under the age of 25 is in the same position," he said.

In his Times interview, Milburn acknowledged that changing the rules for existing claimants would be "difficult politically" but stressed it was necessary.

Disability groups have welcomed extra employment support, but expressed concern that disabled young people could lose out.

'Rebuilding system from scratch'

James Taylor, from disability equality charity Scope, said Pip was a "lifeline" for young disabled people and restricting access to it "won't make young disabled people's extra costs disappear".

Harriet Edwards, from the charity Sense, said changes were "long overdue", but that without additional details families were "deeply anxious" about what they could mean for them.

A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work."

The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.

Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.

Responding on Thursday, Tory shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said Milburn was "right to say it's time to stop handing out cash for mild conditions".

But she raised concern that spending more on work placements would simply "compensate for the jobs Labour have killed with their taxes and red tape".

If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.

The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch", Milburn said.

His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, wherein young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.

In an interview recorded on Tuesday, Skills Minister Jacqui Smith told the BBC that young people had a "responsibility" to take up employment support.

"It is a contract. People need the chance, and they need to take that chance," she added.

A separate review - co-chaired by disabilities minister Sir Stephen Timms - examining disability benefits is also expected to be published this month.

stories.title: Trump wanted little Kei trucks for America, Toyota makes it happen
stories.summary: Does this herald the start of a small car revolution, or is it a meaningless distraction?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Does this herald the start of a small car revolution, or is it a meaningless distraction?

The idea that Americans should be offered a greater choice of smaller cars has support from strange bedfellows indeed. After all, who could forget President Trump—usually one to take a maximalist approach to any problem— announcing last year that he wanted the Department of Transportation to make Japan’s diminutive “Kei” cars legal here in the US.

Ars’ attempts to get DoT to tell us more about the potential influx of little vehicles have mostly fallen on deaf ears. But this week, there has been movement on the topic, with Toyota announcing that it will bring back the Scion brand with the KEI-01.

What’s a Kei car?

In the US, the preponderance of humongous SUVs is a consequence largely of government policies, specifically corporate average fuel economy standards that made it less profitable to sell smaller, efficient cars. Japan’s Kei cars are what happens if the government instead restricts the size, engine capacity, and power output.

A Kei car must fit within the following dimensions: 11.2 feet (3.4 m) long, 4.9 feet (1.5 m) wide, and 6.6 feet (2 m) tall, with an engine displacement of no more than 0.66 L and an output of 63 hp (47 kW) or less. That’s a far cry from the more than 16 feet (4.9 m) of a full-size pickup truck, but it makes sense for a country where you’re not allowed to buy a car unless you have somewhere to park it, with those spaces being at an absolute premium.

Being affordable to buy and economical to run sure doesn’t hurt either, and last year, Japan bought almost 1.7 million Kei cars, out of total sales of 4.6 million vehicles. Depending on where you live in the US, it can be varying degrees of difficult to import a Kei car , at least until now.

Scion is back?

Toyota killed off its Scion sub-brand more than a decade ago , ending the haggle-free approach and cars aimed at younger buyers in favor of selling more Toyotas. But now it’s back as “Scion by Toyota,” which the automaker will apparently use to experiment with less traditional ideas. But forget about a cool-but-boxy EV in the mold of the Honda N-One or Nissan Sakura .

“The future of mobility will not be defined by one vehicle, one technology, or one way of thinking,” said Simon Humphries, Toyota’s chief branding officer and head of design. “Scion by Toyota gives us a place to challenge conventional thinking, explore new possibilities, and create mobility in new ways. The KEI-01, SxS, and BKE concepts each represent a different possibility—and together, they show what can happen when curiosity leads the way.”

Before anyone gets too excited, the KEI-01 will be classified as a “ low-speed vehicle ,” which means it can’t go any faster than 25 mph (40 km/h). So if you were hoping to use one of these but need to drive on anything but surface streets, be prepared to get honked at a lot, and not in a good way. In fact, unless you’re buying a fleet, Toyota won’t sell you a KEI-01 at all, at least not to begin with.

Oh, and it’s only available as right-hand drive, since that’s the side of the road Japan drives on. But it does feature all-wheel drive, so if you own a ranch—or perhaps a whole load of golf courses—the utility becomes a little more obvious. Toyota says the KEI-01 is suited to small business owners in urban environments, farmers and ranchers, organizations that have campuses that need fleets of facility vehicles, delivery drivers, and outdoor enthusiasts. The trucks will be shipped to Toyota’s assembly plant in Indiana as knock-down kits, adding 50 jobs to the plant in mid-2027.

Low-speed vehicles have been street-legal in parts of the US for many years now. In my neighborhood in Washington, DC, Circuit operates a low-speed EV shuttle on demand, and gas-powered golf carts are very popular in retirement communities. Pricing for the KEI-01 hasn’t been announced, but speculation runs from as little as $10,000 to as much as $28,000.

You would not want to drive a vehicle with a maximum speed of 25 mph on a street with a 35-40 mph speed limit. Traveling much more slowly than the surrounding traffic is asking for an accident! And most small cities and towns have many such streets. That is why so many people are bemoaning the low speed of the vehicle; it makes it impractical in places where it would otherwise make a nice small city vehicle. No one's upset that it can't go on the Interstate; they're upset that you couldn't safely drive it around town.

Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.

On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% quarterly growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession.

Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, driven by the rollout of AI.

Underneath the bonnet, growth is being spearheaded by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment.

Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment.

Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices.

However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out.

Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead.

After the US midterm elections and revelations at the chipmaker Nvidia , the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst . A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight.

after newsletter promotion

For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill expected to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year.

In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year.

With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze.

At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

stories.title: MPs urge Labour ministers to get on with trophy hunting ban
stories.summary: It has been over two years since Labour promised to ban imports of the parts of animals hunted for sport.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 hours ago

The government has been accused of dragging its feet on its manifesto promise to ban the import of hunting trophies.

Labour pledged at the 2024 general election to outlaw bringing the parts of animals killed by hunters for sport, such as heads or horns, into the UK.

But it has so far failed to bring a bill enacting the ban to Parliament, and in the two years since the election more than 40 import permits have been granted for hunting trophies.

Speaking during a debate on the subject, Environment Minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter insisted the government was still committed to a ban and a bill would be delivered "when parliamentary time allows".

Labour MP Clive Efford, who had proposed Wednesday's Westminster Hall debate, said the minister's promise "really is not good enough".

"Who is the government afraid of?" he asked, arguing that only a "tiny minority of people" opposed the ban.

He continued: "This issue has been debated widely, over a great many years; there is not much more that we can learn from either side of the argument - this is the time that the government have to act and move forwards."

A ban was first proposed by the Conservative government in 2019, and in 2022 a bill implementing a ban was passed by MPs but ran out of time in the House of Lords.

Conservative MP Henry Smith, who sponsored that bill, accused peers of using "parliamentary devices" to block its passage into law.

During Wednesday's debate, several MPs urged the government to restart the process by introducing a fresh bill to Parliament.

Efford said: "Trophy hunting is not about conservation, it does not resolve issues of wildlife-human conflict, and it does not bring economic benefits to rural areas —certainly not in the way that tourism can.

"Local people have been attacked, their land stolen and their human rights abused. Private companies are stealing their homelands. Britain should not be accommodating this industry."

Labour's Rachael Maskell also called for a ban, but said the government could, in the meantime, make it illegal to advertise safari hunting and make it a criminal offence for UK residents to "celebrate their kill" by posting images on social media.

Labour MP Irene Campbell said she found it "upsetting" that hunting trophies could still be exported from the UK, pointing to an instance of a Scottish stag head being exported to Zimbabwe.

DUP MP Jim Shannon said the flow of hunting trophies coming into the country was continuing at "nearly two dozen a year while the government drag their feet".

Addressing the minister, he said: "I ask her to give us a timescale, give us a date and tell us when [the ban] will happen."

Conservative Roger Gale criticised those who hunted the animals, saying: "A yellow streak runs right through those people and they are revolting."

More than one MP suggested that the government was being pressured by the US not to introduce a ban.

Earlier this year, The Telegraph reported , external that Doug Burgum, the US interior secretary, wrote to the UK government arguing: "Legal, well-regulated hunting – particularly trophy hunting – plays a vital role in supporting healthy wildlife populations, restoring habitat and supporting local economies."

Responding to MPs, Riddell-Carpenter said the government remained committed to banning "the import of hunting trophies from species of conservation concern".

"Our aim is clear: to introduce the bill at the earliest opportunity and within this Parliament," she said, although she declined repeated invitations from MPs to set out a more specific timetable.

Permit conditions

Opponents of the ban argue that it would undermine local economies and reduce the amount of money that could be spent on conservation projects.

The Community Leaders Network, a group of rural representatives from countries in southern Africa, argues that regulated hunting helps pay for rangers and wildlife management.

"In practice, a ban could do the opposite of what it intends: less funding can mean fewer patrols, more poaching, poorer habitat management, and ultimately less wildlife," it says.

An Oxford University report from 2024 concluded , external that a ban would not ease pressure on threatened species, and said around 79% of imports to the UK between 2015 and 2021 had came from countries where hunted species were "stable, increasing or abundant".

Currently it is legal to bring hunting trophies into the UK, as long as there is a permit to do so.

The government has said permits are only issued when "strict conditions" have been met, including demonstrating that their import "will not have a detrimental effect on the conservation status of the species".

Between July 2024 and September 2026, the government issued permits for 41 imports including 21 African elephants, four hippos, five lions, a leopard and a giraffe.

stories.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
stories.summary: Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade , it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia. After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP. stories.title: We’re Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
stories.summary: Today , along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant , a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places. But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin , ALPRs give law enforcement “ a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “ form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment. We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant. Related Cases: Wisconsin Council of Churches v. Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha & Green Bay SIREN and CAIR-CA v. San Jose

stories.body:
‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’

Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.

One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of Democrats ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back Donald Trump ’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.

Early odds suggest a Democrat may win the presidential election in two years, a fitting coda to last week’s broad rejection of the Maga brand of politics. It’s not beyond hope to expect a Democratic trifecta that will spend less time on settling grievances and more on fixing a threadbare social safety net that allows for the deepest poverty in the affluent world .

And yet, the post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money. The federal deficit is now running at about 6.2% of GDP . The federal debt hit $40tn, more than 120% of the nation’s gross domestic product. Paying interest on that debt costs some 3.2% of GDP. That’s about $1tn, more than is spent on national defense. The Congressional Budget Office projects that debt and interest payments will continue to grow faster than the economy over the coming decades. In October alone, the first month of the 2027 fiscal year, the fiscal deficit ballooned to $409bn.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that restoring the subsidies to health insurance plans under Obamacare from 2030 to 2039 would cost $460bn. Undoing the budget cuts to the Snap food stamp program and Medicaid that Trump used to partly fund the tax cuts in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would cost $2.2tn over that decade. “Reversing the harms is going to be very expensive,” said CBPP’s senior director for Federal budget policy, Brendan Duke.

And that’s the easy part. The trust fund that pays for social security benefits is scheduled to run out of money in less than six years, when the new crop of Democratic senators are still in their first term. By law, that would lead to an automatic 22% cut in benefits. Fixing that will require more money. Artificial intelligence may further complicate the picture, burdening the safety net with potentially millions of workers displaced by the new technological revolution.

Historian Bruce Bartlett, who back in the day advised Ronald Reagan on budget policy, argues that this state of affairs is the outcome of a Republican strategy honed over the years since Gipper’s day: cut taxes to strangle the budget and tie the hands of whatever Democratic administration comes next.

Trump’s OBBBA will add somewhere between $4.1tn and $5.5tn to the federal debt over 10 years, depending on whether temporary tax cuts in the bill are made permanent by a future Congress, something that has usually happened in the past. This, Bartlett once told me , will “make sure the next Democratic president is a complete and total failure”.

The new taxes that would be needed just to fill the holes Trump and his Republican enablers bored into the budget, let alone patch up the safety net they gleefully eviscerated, seem beyond anything achieved in recent memory.

Consider this: The last time that a government with any Republican in power delivered a tax increase was in the 1990s, when George HW Bush was president and Congress was blue. Bush paid for his sin, though, losing reelection to Democrat Bill Clinton. And that was the end of that.

Democrats have raised money when they held the presidency and Congress. But the trend suggests the opportunities are fading. Bill Clinton’s 1993 tax increases are estimated to yield the equivalent of $3.3tn over the 2030-2039 decade, adjusting for inflation. But the feat, which helped produce the nation’s first budget surplus since the 1960s, was ultimately spent on a tax cut by Clinton’s successor, George W. Bush.

The next shot at raising taxes was more modest. Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act raised the equivalent of $1.1tn over 2030-2039, in inflation-adjusted dollars. But Obama also made permanent some of George W Bush’s tax cuts. Joe Biden tried to go bigger: his original Build Back Better Act, passed in the House, would have raised the equivalent of $2.3tn over that window. But the Senate nixed that, authorizing only about $700bn in the Inflation Reduction Act.

How much more tax revenue does the US need? It depends on what Democrats want to achieve. Total tax revenue in the US amounts to less than 26% of its gross domestic product. That is 9 percentage points less than Britain’s total tax take, as a share of its economy, 9.5 points less than Canada’s, 12.5 points less than Germany’s and 16 percentage points less than Sweden’s.

Perhaps matching other rich countries is an impossibly high bar. Still, Democrats must prove that they understand the new America they hope to build comes with a price tag they are willing to fight for.

Some tax cuts in Trump’s OBBBA are set to expire in the next couple of years: exemptions on income from tips and overtime, a new deduction for seniors and an increase in the deduction for state and local taxes. The CBPP observed that these cuts offer next to nothing to Americans on the bottom rungs of the income distribution. Extending them would cost about $1.2tn over the 10-year window.

Will Democrats have the guts to end them? That will be the test of whether America is ready for a new social contract or not.

stories.title: Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?
stories.summary: Chief financial officer Colette Kress in in charge of Nvidia for now, but several others are in the frame as potential successors.

stories.body:
Arm's boss Rene Haas (L), Nvidia's Colette Kress (C) and Chris Malachowsky (R) have been named as possible successors

Published 12 November 2026, 10:37 GMT

Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.

The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.

We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.

The finance chief

Colette Kress is chief financial officer at Nvidia

Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.

Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.

She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.

But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.

The co-founder and the engineer

Chris Malachowsky is one of Nvidia's three co-founders

Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.

Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.

Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.

Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.

"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.

Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.

Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced.

Apple and Arm's top brass

Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.

Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.

Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.

Apple's Tim Cook (R) with Jensen Huang (L) and his wife Lori Huang at the White House

Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant.

Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung.

Rene Haas is the boss of Arm Holdings

Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana.

"The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said.

What now for Nvidia?

Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive.

"The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies."

Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company.

An early indication came as markets opened in New York shortly after Huang's resignation was announced.

Nvidia shares opened down more than 13%, wiping more than half a trillion dollars off the firm's share market value.

Jensen Huang's departure leaves a void in the influential AI giant

Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here".

Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines."

Ray Wang, chief executive of Constellation Research, said the crisis isn't so much an issue for the wider AI industry but rather one for Nvidia itself which has to consider if the person it appoints as its chief executive has the same appeal as Huang.

"That's really what the issue is, because a lot of these partnerships and investments have been made because of the trust with with Jensen," he said.

stories.body:
The behaviour of every atom, and so all of biology and chemistry as we know them, depends on the mass of the electron.

Electrons are one of the fundamental particles (the very smallest building blocks of nature) that make up the atom. They orbit the atom’s central nucleus, which is made up of proton and neutron particles. The mass of the electron is very small, contributing little to the mass of the atom, but it is vital for determining an atom’s size .

If the mass of the electron was made significantly lighter or heavier, it would affect not only the size of the atom, but also the way that chemistry works throughout the universe – potentially making biology impossible.

Physicists have never confirmed how the electron acquires its mass. But a proposed collider at Cern, in Geneva, could finally put that to the test.

The masses of fundamental particles span an enormous range. The current best theory to explain fundamental physics, known as the Standard Model , offers no explanation for this. So testing the origin of particle masses offers a crucial check on this theory. It could also point researchers towards new discoveries in physics.

In 1964, the Edinburgh-based physicist Peter Higgs and fellow researchers proposed that fundamental particles obtain their mass by interacting with a new field. In physics, a field is a physical quantity that has a value assigned to each point in space and time, like the temperatures dotted across a weather map. An object interacting with a field is influenced by the field’s value at its location.

The stronger the interaction between a fundamental particle and this field, the heavier the particle will be. This idea became the heart of the Standard Model. It took nearly 50 years, and the construction of the largest machine ever built – the Large Hadron Collider at Cern, the European laboratory for particle physics – to confirm the existence of the Higgs boson.

The discovery of this particle confirmed that nature uses the mass-generating mechanism proposed by Peter Higgs and others back in the 60s. This momentous achievement led to Higgs and fellow pioneering physicist François Englert sharing the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics .

Fundamental particles, like the electron, cannot be broken down into smaller parts. But they can combine to form composite particles, such as the proton and neutron that form the nucleus of an atom. The Standard Model describes twelve fundamental matter particles.

Six are called quarks and include the “up” and “down” quarks that make up protons and neutrons. The other six are called leptons, one of which is the electron.

The masses of these fundamental particles have a puzzling hierarchy. For example, the heaviest, the top quark, has a mass 300,000 times larger than the electron, and 40 times larger than the next heaviest quark.

While the Standard Model can explain how particles obtain mass, it offers no explanation for why these masses span such an enormous range. This is one of several reasons why particle physicists believe that there must be physics beyond the Standard Model that has not yet been explored.

Challenging measurement

New theories could modify our picture of how fundamental particles obtain mass, making it important to use experiments to test the mechanism proposed by Higgs and others. At the Large Hadron Collider, we have verified it for the heaviest particles, and we are close to doing so for the muon, a heavier cousin of the electron.

However, the electron interacts incredibly weakly with the Higgs field, making it too difficult to measure at current colliders. This leaves open the question of whether the Higgs mechanism is responsible for its mass.

To close this gap in our knowledge, physicists have proposed using FCC-ee, the first stage of a planned $19 billion physics machine called the Future Circular Collider , which could follow the Large Hadron Collider in the 2040s.

Most fundamental particles have a corresponding antiparticle – another sub-atomic particle that has the same mass but a different electric charge. FCC-ee would accelerate electrons and their corresponding antiparticles (known as positrons) around a 91km-long ring underneath the French-Swiss border, before colliding the two beams of particles inside detectors. These detectors are specialised experiments that can track and measure the particles produced when the beams crash into one another.

FCC-ee has a key advantage over proton-proton colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider: smashing together electrons and positrons can directly produce a Higgs boson. By looking for this process, we can probe the strength of the electron-Higgs interaction.

Detecting new particles

In principle, the measurement is simple: collide electrons with positrons and count the Higgs bosons produced. In practice, it is very challenging. To produce enough Higgs bosons, the collider would need to run for a few years at an energy extremely close to the mass of the Higgs boson particle.

However, that’s a long time to run this machine in such a specialised way. The measurement also relies on us knowing the Higgs mass much more precisely than we do today. Detecting the Higgs bosons is another challenge, because many unrelated processes can mimic the desired signal.

In a recent preprint (which has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal) on this topic, a team of physicists assumed that the Higgs bosons decay (or transform) into W bosons, another fundamental particle with a lower mass. They used a machine learning algorithm to distinguish the desired signal from other processes. In simulations, they found that this approach could improve sensitivity to the electron-Higgs interaction by nearly a factor of 200 compared with current limits at the Large Hadron Collider.

However, new theories could modify interactions between the electron and the Higgs field, including through the action of previously undiscovered particles. But these theories would also need to fit with the known, previously measured properties of the electron. This is what my collaborators and I studied in a recent paper , where we examined how new particles can change the way the electron interacts with the Higgs field.

Our findings suggest that many candidates for such hypothetical particles, such as new, heavy versions of the electron, can be indirectly searched for in planned measurements of the magnetic properties of the electron. These tests will be carried out by several different physics experiments around the world.

However, one potential new particle is a different form of the Higgs boson that interacts mainly with electrons. If this exists, the Future Circular Collider will be in a unique position to test its properties and how it affects the electron.

This story captures the interplay between theory and experiment when planning new colliders. Theorists map out the new physics a measurement could detect, so experimentalists know when a result would be decisive.

This proposed run of the FCC-ee isn’t yet confirmed and many of the new physics models it could test can be probed in other ways. But a new, electron-loving form of Higgs boson would first show up here. Either way, this measurement would tell us something we’ve never known: how the electron, one of the most studied particles in nature, truly gets its mass.

stories.body:
Collagen is turning up in coffee, crisps and beauty creams, promising firmer skin and stronger joints. As someone who studies collagen, I find some of the claims rather optimistic.

I even gave collagen supplements to guests at my wedding, accompanied by a disclaimer that this was no endorsement of their effectiveness. The science is considerably more interesting than the marketing.

Collagen is a family of at least 28 proteins that help give the body its shape and strength. All share a distinctive structure: three chains twisted together, rather like strands of a rope. Some of these molecules assemble into larger fibres around cells that support skin, tendons and bones. Other types form thin supporting networks separating different body compartments.

Collagen is part of the extracellular matrix, the mesh of proteins and other materials surrounding our cells. Cells make collagen using amino acids, the building blocks of all proteins, and release it outside themselves to build and maintain tissues.

As we age, keeping this structure in good repair becomes harder. The amount of collagen produced can change, but existing collagen also becomes altered. Some fibres last extraordinarily long: carbon-dating research suggests the central part of the human Achilles tendon contains collagen laid down during the first 17 years of life, with very little replacement in adulthood.

Over time, chemical bonds can form between collagen molecules making the tissue less flexible. So having more collagen does not necessarily mean having healthier collagen. How it is assembled, maintained and replaced also matters.

Does eating collagen replenish it?

Many supplements contain hydrolysed collagen: collagen that has already been broken into smaller pieces. Gelatine, familiar from gummy sweets, is another processed form of collagen.

After you swallow collagen, digestion breaks it down further into amino acids and short chains called peptides. Some of these reach the bloodstream . But they do not arrive in your cheeks or knees as ready-made collagen fibres. Cells may reuse those building blocks to make proteins, or for other purposes.

So is collagen powder any better than getting enough protein from ordinary food? It’s an important question, and one we cannot yet answer confidently.

Human trials of oral collagen supplements have produced mixed results. A 2025 analysis of 23 trials found improvements in skin hydration and elasticity overall, but no statistically significant benefits when higher-quality studies were examined separately. A newer review of 35 trials reported improvements in hydration and some measures of elasticity, but found no reliable evidence of reduced wrinkles or increased skin density. These findings do not establish whether taking collagen offers any advantage over eating an adequate, balanced diet.

Bone broth is another source of collagen-derived protein. I enjoy it as part of the diet I grew up eating, but swallowing broth does not specifically replace collagen in your joints, at least not evidenced by science . Its nutritional value depends on the ingredients and preparation.

Can creams and treatments do more?

Collagen creams face another obstacle: the skin is a protective barrier. Intact collagen molecules are generally too large to pass through it . A cream may make your skin feel smoother by helping it retain water without delivering new collagen to deeper layers.

There is better evidence for protecting the collagen you already have. Ultraviolet radiation from sunlight can increase collagen breakdown , making sunscreen important. Studies also suggest that retinoids , ingredients related to vitamin A, can improve fine wrinkles and stimulate collagen production, although they can irritate skin.

I’m also cautious about skincare containing PDRN, fragments of DNA often promoted as being derived from salmon sperm. A review of clinical trials suggests PDRN may help damaged skin heal, including by speeding up wound repair.

But these findings don’t necessarily apply to ordinary face creams. Wounded skin has a damaged protective barrier, whereas healthy skin makes it much harder for large molecules such as PDRN to penetrate. Whether enough PDRN can reach the deeper layers of intact skin to produce meaningful benefits remains uncertain .

Microneedling works differently. Tiny needles create controlled injuries, setting off repair processes that can stimulate collagen formation. Clinical studies suggest benefits for some acne scars , but the procedure can cause infection, pigmentation changes or further scarring , especially when hygiene and technique are poor.

Home microneedling rollers – handheld devices covered in tiny needles that are rolled across the skin – also carry risks . Pressing too hard or repeatedly treating the same area can damage the skin, potentially causing lasting discolouration or scarring. Poorly cleaned devices can introduce bacteria, while rolling over infected areas can spread viruses such as herpes across the skin.

The American Academy of Dermatology also warns that home devices generally produce less noticeable results than professional treatments, so the potential benefits may be limited.

The surprising connection with sleep

My research has found that collagen maintenance follows a daily rhythm in mouse tendons . The animals’ cells produced and assembled collagen at different times, and disrupting their internal body clocks affected the fibres they formed.

Later work showed that cells can take up existing collagen and recycle it into new fibres . This recycling process was altered in cells associated with fibrosis, a condition in which excessive scar-like tissue builds up in an organ.

In the lungs, this can make breathing difficult. These are early findings about how tissues maintain collagen, not proof that a particular bedtime will improve human skin, although it is clear that sleep disruption wreaks havoc on our body in general.

Nor does eating collagen cause fibrosis. The point is that the body must regulate how much collagen it makes and how it organises and removes it.

For now, I would prioritise a balanced diet, physical activity, consistent sleep and sun protection over expensive promises to “boost collagen”. Looking after the systems that maintain our tissues is more sensible than assuming a scoop of powder will rebuild them.
