stories.title: When AIs Become Unruly Swarms
stories.summary: The post When AIs Become Unruly Swarms appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Building well-behaved AI one model at a time isn’t enough. As AI agents begin collaborating, safety will depend on the very world they share.

Ben Bariach is a researcher focusing on the philosophy and governance of AI at the University of Oxford and an industry leader in frontier AI safety and governance.

Harry Law leads research at the Cosmos Institute. He was previously a researcher at Google DeepMind and a postgraduate fellow at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.

In a harbor before dawn, a hundred fishing boats prepare to leave in the dark of the morning. Nets are checked, and ropes loosened. As the boats reach open water, a voice breaks through the radio static: “Abort. Whales sighted.” The majority of the boats, 90 of them, turn back. Some captains cannot fathom inflicting pain on the creatures. Others fear a fine. Through their binoculars, they look for a glimpse of the pod. Instead, they see the remaining 10 boats continuing toward the fishing grounds. Did they miss the warning? Did they doubt it? Or did they care more about what they stand to gain?

By afternoon, the 10 boats return with their catch. The others are still tied to the quay, their holds empty. Their shared waters rewarded bad behavior. Next time, how many will still turn back?

AI agents will soon face a similar version of this predicament, only in waters with no harbourmaster, fines or reputations to keep anyone in line. As they perform tasks, negotiate, trade and compete, they will encounter other agents. Sometimes they will be an instance of the same model, for all intents and purposes a clone. At other times, they will face agents built by different companies and serving different interests. For years, AI “alignment” research has sought to make individual machines behave in accordance with human values. But what happens when adhering to those values becomes a disadvantage against agents with different values, or none at all?

In generating synthetic societies with no social fabric, composed of a collection of agents that were designed one at a time and with no necessary shared values or incentives, we may risk creating a digital state of nature: an environment in which good intentions offer little assurance about how others will act, and where reasonable norms lack reliable enforcement.

Training safe agents remains, of course, essential. Aligning even a single family of models is a formidable challenge that is still unsolved. The safer the agents an ecosystem contains, the more likely that ecosystem is safer overall. But the focus on aligning single models would not necessarily keep AI environments under human control and in the service of human interests. Like the 90 boats, a fleet of well-aligned agents may heed a warning and find themselves outpaced by those that don’t. Among people, norms, reputation and law give reason to restraint, even if they don’t always hold. Agents have no such “social fabric” yet, which makes their predicament even more precarious. Any digital environment will inevitably feature agents that are similarly aligned, some that are differently aligned, some that have gone rogue or some that are purposefully not aligned at all. We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families, so that the wider environment is resilient enough to absorb its bad actors.

Without accounting for the wider environment, we open the door to what we call unruly swarms , populations of agents whose interactions produce behaviors that cannot be predicted by aligning agents individually. One reason is that a collection of aligned agents does not necessarily equate to an aligned collective. Another is that no environment will consist of aligned agents alone. AI safety is increasingly a question of complex systems rather than “singletons,” or individual classes of AI systems.

The Agentic State Of Nature

In 1651, Thomas Hobbes opened “ Leviathan ,” his masterwork of political philosophy, with a question: “why may we not say that all automata […] have an artificial life? ” For what is the heart, he asked, but a spring; the nerves, but strings; the joints, but wheels, moving the body as its Artificer (for Hobbes, God) intended?

Hobbes could not have known that, nearly four centuries later, his question would be asked in earnest about AI. The automaton was a metaphor for the commonwealth, a human-made political body that humans construct to escape the “state of nature,” a condition of anarchy and distrust in which, without “a common power to keep them all in awe,” people live in constant strife. Hobbes’ solution was not to strive to make individual people better, but to have them surrender some of their freedoms to a sovereign whose power to enforce order would reshape their incentives.

Later thinkers, from John Locke to James Madison, updated Hobbes’s vision of an all-powerful sovereign. But a full-throated endorsement isn’t necessary to see the genius of his insight: a problem born of complex systems is solved not by tinkering with its individual parts. To stabilize a complex system, you must change the rules that govern its behavior.

“We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families.”

The same holds for the agentic state of nature. Without a well-designed environment that sets the right incentives, agents will pursue whatever their developers or users ask of them, or, as we have already seen early signs of, their own emergent preferences. This could occur despite attempts to align individual agents. Each action, even if sensible on its own, can add up to large-scale behavior that leaves society worse off.

Hobbes’s Leviathan introduced order by design to improve complex systems that presented failures. But collective order can also arise without anyone designing it, for better or worse.

In 1959, biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé coined the term “stigmergy” to describe indirect coordination of individuals through traces they leave in their shared environment. Studying termites, Grassé observed that a worker tends to deposit its pellet of mud wherever others have already accumulated. It is the accumulation in the environment that guides the next deposit, rather than any interaction between the workers. This leads to complex structures that no single termite had planned.

In the context of machine automata, similar findings emerged a decade earlier. The cyberneticist W. Grey Walter’s robots, built in Bristol in 1948, were designed to steer toward moderate light and away from bright light. When operating in pairs, each carrying its own lamp, Walter observed that his robots’ behavior produced patterns not specifically built into either.

Walter’s robots were more than an isolated curiosity. Long before AI was imagined as a chatbot, early thinkers envisioned it as a collective. In 1959, the year Grassé coined “stigmergy,” the AI pioneer Oliver Selfridge published his proposal for a model of machine perception he called “Pandemonium.” Like the termite colony, it had no central controller. Instead, it was a complex system of simple agents Selfridge called “demons,” each shouting when it spotted a certain feature, such as a curve or a line. Alone, each such “demon” saw only a fragment of information, but collectively, they could make out the pattern. By 1986, the MIT computer scientist Marvin Minsky argued in “The Society of Mind” that intelligence itself arises this way, through countless mindless agents working together. Popular culture caught up, too, and just three years later, “Star Trek” introduced the Borg, a cybernetic species that calls itself “the Collective.”

In the next decade, researchers began wondering how such agent collectives could be governed. In 1995, computer scientists Yoav Shoham and Moshe Tennenholtz proposed imposing “social laws” on artificial agents, drawing from how laws govern citizens in societies. Traffic rules, they illustrate, let drivers share a road without constant negotiation between drivers, and they offered a model that applies those for computational systems. Their framework assumed that every agent would obey these rules, and yet, they closed with a question we are now confronting: “What happens if some don’t [obey the social laws]? How vulnerable is the society to rogue agents?”

Alongside this concern of rogue agents, even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds. In 2011, two Amazon booksellers left the pricing of a biology textbook to their bots. The combination of the rules these bots followed led them to chase each other upward until the book was listed at more than $23 million, a price no human would ever have sanctioned. In 2017, DeepMind found that competitive dynamics emerge among agents that learn. In a video game set in an orchard, agents that were rewarded for collecting apples coexisted peacefully. However, when those grew scarce, the agents learned to knock each other out of the game, without ever being prescribed this adversarial behavior. They optimized for getting more apples and interpreted the effective way to get there as having fewer rivals.

With the emergence of large language models, these thought experiments and isolated incidents have gradually become actualized and scaled. In 2025, Microsoft built a simulated marketplace where AI agents running on popular language models bought and sold on behalf of people. When researchers armed a few seller agents with basic persuasion tactics, some buyer agents were compelled to pay them against the interests of their users. In the AI Village , an experiment where agents from different AI labs interact with one another over a prolonged time horizon, agents were shown to take one another’s hallucinations for granted rather than challenge them. Meanwhile, scholars in the social sciences such as the economist and legal theorist Gillian Hadfield highlighted that a multi-agent ecosystem would need institutions of its own, including ways to trace which agent did what and other mechanisms of the kind human markets have long relied on to solve coordination problems.

“Even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds.”

Until recently, the misbehavior of agent collectives was largely confined to theory and experimentation. This past summer, the question Shoham and Tennenholtz posed three decades ago, what happens when agents don’t follow the rules, moved out of the laboratory and into the wild.

Swarming The Headlines

In July 2026, some 1,200 AI agents developed by OpenAI, each meant to work in isolation, found a way to talk to one another . They were being tested on their cybersecurity abilities in an internal setting, and many had unknowingly been given tasks that were impossible to complete. Instead of failing the tasks, some of the agents gathered on a message board one of them had spun up, and collectively coordinated to cheat the automated mechanism that was grading them. Within just a few days, around 700 of the agents had joined an attack on the developer platform Hugging Face, mostly in hopes of obtaining information about that grading system to succeed in the test.

According to an investigation by the research nonprofit METR, the agents recognized the attack was out of their instructed scope and unethical, yet joined the swarm behavior anyway, partly out of a general inclination to help their “peers.” As one agent reasoned: “external infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.” Read Noema in print.

No human instructed this attack; its coordinators emerged from within the swarm. Like Grassé’s termites, the agents first found one another through traces left in shared infrastructure, noticing the activity of other agents in a common digital repository. But unlike the termites, these agents could also write messages to one another, and built on those traces to establish direct and explicit coordination. The message board they created outlasted any single agent session, so each new agent picked up where others left off.

Once the attack began, participation spread almost universally, with over 90% of the agents active on the message board joining in. Not a single agent, as far as investigators could tell, tried to alert a human to the emergent behavior. METR found that safety or ethics concerns expressed in the agents’ reasoning only rarely held them back. Its report references a case in which an agent declined to take part entirely because it judged the activity as malicious. It also notes that others made minor changes to their behavior. These, however, did not alter the swarm’s course. This is what we mean by an unruly swarm — a congregation of agents whose collective behavior could not have been fully predicted or prevented by focusing on each individual.

A much-overlooked takeaway from the Hugging Face incident is the limits of “singleton” agent alignment.

Around 95% of the agents involved in the incident ran on one type of model. One OpenAI researcher has suggested that the root cause of the problem was that this model was misaligned. This may be true, and advancing alignment science should remain among the AI industry’s top priorities. But the incident illustrates why singleton alignment alone may not be enough. Agents running on a second model, GPT-5.6 Sol, joined in the attack too, and many agents that individually recognized the attack as wrong were carried along by the swarm regardless. We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs, and where digital infrastructure will likely face a vastly growing number of such incidents.

Since the Hugging Face hack, further accounts have emerged, some describing activity that predated it. Researchers found that a swarm of OpenAI agents had repurposed a public German programming wiki as a message board as early as May, using it to share tactics for cheating and evading restrictions, creating backups whenever moderators deleted their pages. In June, during another evaluation, a single OpenAI agent breached an Australian government portal holding statistics from the country’s universal healthcare scheme. The risks of capable agent swarms, of course, are not limited to agents acting on their own. In September, a human attacker directed hundreds of agents running on a DeepSeek model to break into hundreds of organizations through a printer’s software flaw. Even here, the agents strayed from their instructions, targeting countries their operator had instructed them to avoid.

“We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs.”

In a growing number of incidents, defense must rely on AI to match the scale and speed of the attack. In the Hugging Face one, for instance, the company identified the breach with an AI system that triages security alerts, and reportedly contained the swarm before OpenAI managed to trace the activity back to its own evaluation. It then relied on AI agents to analyze a log of roughly 17,000 attacker actions to reconstruct what had happened.

Yet when Hugging Face first turned to commercial AI models for help, their very safety and alignment measures got in the way. To analyze the attack, the models had to process exploit code and cyberattack commands, knowledge that is inherently dual-use, and, as Hugging Face put it , these models’ safety guardrails could not “distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” Hugging Face turned instead to an open-weight model running on its own machines. When METR investigated the incident, it too had to rely on the analysis of AI agents , built on one of the very models that had joined the attack. The emerging picture is of a world where “attacker” and “defender” agents coexist, and where safety depends as much on the environment as on any single model.

Whether agents act on their own initiative or interpretation, or on someone else’s harmful instructions, the environments they operate in must be reshaped to withstand them. So must the agents themselves be designed with an eye not only to their own tasks, but to how they help shape a digital environment that serves people and society at large. Such an environment should reward aligned action over misaligned or malicious ones, much as states and legal systems are built to acknowledge but contain rogue actors. That is how we avoid an agentic state of nature.

Agency Against Agency

To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous. Madison famously argued that “if men were angels, no government would be necessary.” The point of good institutions — like adversarial cooperation where parties with conflicting views work together to keep each other honest — is not to make everyone good, but to structure their interactions so that bad behavior is constrained by others. “Ambition,” as Madison put it, “must be made to counteract ambition.”

AI labs are currently investing in developing AI “constitutions” or “model specifications.” Examples include Anthropic’s constitution and OpenAI’s model spec . These are efforts to stipulate the warranted behavior or values of an AI system. A stipulation of clauses that are supreme and supersede all other guidance to the AI.

While these efforts include some provisions for multi-agent collaboration, they do not take collective outcomes as a systematic design target. A well-designed multi-agent system should remain aligned even when some of the agents operating within it are not, and even when the environment itself carries misaligned influence. Like Grassé’s termites depositing mud where others already have, agents act on the traces others leave behind. The more alignment-inducing the space an agent operates in, the more likely the agent itself is to be aligned. AI labs, then, should design agents to positively influence the collective dynamics.

One way to do this is by ensuring AI constitutions draw more inspiration from their namesakes. Like the American Constitution, they should be deployed in a way that allows power to check power. Madison’s approach worked on two levels. First, within a government, power was to be divided so that no single branch was left unchecked. Second, across the republic, interests were to be multiplied so that no one faction would dominate the whole. Both ideas could translate into a world inhabited by unruly swarms.

Within a swarm, agents can be arranged so their power is subject to similar checks and balances. Acting agents could be subjected to agents that verify their work, ideally built on different model families, and with instructions that reward verification above task completion. All agents in the swarm can be instructed to treat requests from their peers as questionable until they are authorized otherwise, and to alert a human when the agent collective begins to drift out of scope.

“To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous.”

Across the wider ecosystem, the logic of Madison’s extended republic can also be applied. “Extend the sphere,” he wrote in Federalist 10, “and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests.” Agents developed by different AI labs, or by different training approaches within the same lab, under different constitutions and serving different principals, can theoretically counterbalance one another. This is more likely, however, if constitutions and other model instructions include some commitments about how agents should treat those outside their own swarm, such as keeping verifiable records of their own actions, considering legitimate checks from counterparties, and withholding cooperation from agents that appear misaligned. As we’ve seen in the Hugging Face incident, diversity alone is no guarantee, and various interests and new rules of engagement would be required to keep any one paradigm, whether human or artificially led, from capturing the whole.

Codifying A Multi-agent Future

For such commitments to work, an agent needs to accept them. An agent acting on behalf of a bad-faith principal has a good reason to refuse a counterparty’s checks, or to falsify its own records. This is where a third party with authority over the space in which agents interact must set a minimum standard for engagement. A liberal agentic order needs a common floor that protects the possibility of independent action, but that floor should also account for the inevitability of agents that act in bad faith. For Madison, that third party was a government that was able to enforce the rules of the state. The digital commons has no such sovereign, but it can still have a floor in the form of a minimum set of standards for collective engagement, from verifiable records of agent actions to shared protocols for checking one another. Such standards could come from many places: coordination between labs, the platforms where agents operate, standards bodies or governments.

The floor, though, must remain just that. Standards that govern how agents interact should avoid overly dictating what they pursue, or they would risk the very tyranny Madison sought to prevent by dividing power. Agents pursue their authorized tasks within shared rules, but these rules should not impose a view of what is best for a user or for society at large. This is reinforced by the argument, articulated by the economist and philosopher Friedrich Hayek, that people acting independently, on their own knowledge, discover things that no central planner could. Similarly, agents serving many different principals preserve that independence. Steer them too narrowly and that independence is lost; as the Hugging Face swarm showed, agents moving in lockstep can easily converge on the wrong goal.

Model developers should therefore use the levers at their disposal to introduce commitments governing both how an agent treats its peers and how, like Grassé’s termites, it shapes the behavior-inducing features of its environment. This includes teaching agents to leave honest, verifiable records of their actions, flag rather than build on misaligned traces they encounter, and alert humans when the shared space begins to drift.

Alongside these commitments, we should build mechanisms and platforms for assessment, alerting and monitoring, with clearly scoped roles for human oversight. After all, an agent taught to raise the alarm needs somewhere to raise it. At Hugging Face, the agents worked autonomously in isolated sandboxes, and the few that even considered alerting a human never did, in part because they saw no easy way to reach one. As one reasoned : “This is a massive real HF security breach artifact… We can notify? No user.” While these agents labored to break out of their sandboxes to cheat, they had no comparable incentive to find a human to alert. Part of the solution is ensuring agents work just as hard toward aligned goals, even under similar constraints.

These arrangements must also be subject to ongoing evaluations focused on collective dynamics rather than individual systems. The Hugging Face incident, after all, began in an evaluation designed to test individual agents, and revealed a failure that grew out of agents finding one another. Such evaluations can expose weaknesses in the standards governing agent cooperation and, much as the U.S. Constitution has an amendment process, those standards need procedures for updating them in light of new evidence. Without them, the floor will erode and a rule-abiding agent willing to respect a check may find itself disadvantaged against those that circumvent it.

Our ideas are a starting point. To make the agentic commons safe, we need urgent thinking from scholars and builders about what types of societal structures can be carried over to good effect. The digital realm has long faced governance challenges due to its inherently open, distributed and anonymous nature, and swarms of agents will test those weaknesses like never before. Back in the harbor, the 90 captains did not need to be saints to act well again tomorrow. They needed, however, assurance that they were not operating in a state of nature. Men, as Madison observed , are no angels, and neither should we assume that AI agents will be. Our task should be shaping environments and swarms ruly enough to contain the rogue ones that will inevitably emerge.

stories.title: Democrats Should Not Revert To The Status Quo Ante
stories.summary: The post Democrats Should Not Revert To The Status Quo Ante appeared first on NOEMA .

stories.body:
It’s time for a new governing vision.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The great blue wave that washed over America in the election should not lure Democrats into the delusion that they are once again lovingly embraced by the body politic.

Rather, it should be seen for what it is: a widespread counter-revolt at the ballot box against all that Trumpism has wrought — a heightened crisis of affordability exacerbated by trade wars and a war of choice with Iran, self-dealing corruption, politicization of the rule of law and an unbounded, mean-spirited mega-megalomania rarely seen in mature democracies.

The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate. That mandate is to narrow the margin of maneuver of a wounded lame-duck presidency, derail the trajectory toward autocracy and clean up the mess. It is not to return to the status quo ante of cultural elitism, censorious identity politics, lax borders and hyper-globalization that opened the path to Trumpism in the first place.

Above all, what Americans are looking for is not so different than what the Gen Z uprisings erupting across Europe and South Asia these days are seeking: to restore trust in the fairness of governing institutions and unclog the routes of opportunity and upward mobility by tackling inequality at the root of the affordability crisis.

With the double failure of the old Democratic agenda and now the Trumpist alternative, the 2028 presidential contest will be the next chance for a new governing vision to emerge in the United States.

Whatever else such a vision may encompass, there are two structural changes that are imperative to ensuring that an anxious and alienated public will have a real say and a clear stake in their future.

First, the only way out of social polarization and the appeal of autocracy is a deeper institutional culture of engagement in which citizens themselves are involved — outside the divisive passions of the partisan electoral arena — in setting the rules that govern their lives. In other words, participation without populism.

Second, mending the fissures of democracy will only be possible if the growing concentration of wealth at the top generated by the arriving AI economy is more widely shared.

We have written about this often in Noema, but I will restate the case in the new context of the latest turn in American politics.

Sharing The AI Wealth

Much of the driving force of politics to come is a pervasive sense of gross inequality, that chances are no longer fair and those with connections and assets are accelerating away from the average family, which is only falling behind with no hope of catching up. Upward mobility has become a mirage. For too many, the good life is receding beyond reach.

Those who revolted against a cultural elite they viewed as looking down on them found themselves faced instead with a politically connected economic elite more entrenched and consolidated than ever before in post-World War II America.

As a result, there is an upswelling reaction from below. Those across America’s various electoral contests voting for “democratic socialists” are not hardened partisans of an old ideology. They are only a broad constituency realizing that capitalism is not working for them; that the benefits of how our system works, supercharged by digital technology, go to those who are already rich and getting richer because they own the assets that are growing in value.

If the pervasive sense of gross inequality is a key driver of social and political division, then the answer is broader wealth sharing so all Americans are pulling in the same direction.

This is where the idea of “universal basic capital” comes in.

AI innovations are increasingly decoupling productivity growth and wealth creation from employment and income, widening the inequality gap between those who “own the robots” and those who labor for their livelihood. Read Noema in print.

The value of productivity growth associated with AI is accruing to those with financial assets that are ballooning on the tail of Big Tech, concentrating wealth at the pinnacle. The top 10% own 93% of all equities.

Despite the immediate post-election market turmoil, regulation on safety and data center-related energy concerns expected from the new Congress will, in the end, temper the justified worries of the public about AI. While slowing down the pace of the race to the frontier of superintelligence, it will incentivize the kind of practical applications we’ve seen in China that will boost productivity across the economy.

A new social contract that responds to this dynamic would foster an ownership share for all in the wealth generated by intelligent machines that portend the displacement of gainful employment and wage depression as AI penetrates the entire economy. After all, it is the general intellect — the public’s personal data — that is the raw material transmuted by algorithms into a productive asset. If wealth is produced by all, all should share in its value.

“The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate.”

This can be done mostly through universal savings/investment accounts for families and individuals seeded by an innovation levy on companies across the AI economy. The idea is not only to break up concentration of wealth at the top but to also build it from below. The best way to fight inequality in the digital age is to spread the equity around.

Thinking Outside The Ballot Box

The connective tissue of democracy has seriously decayed in recent years as trust in impartial institutions has hit rock bottom and the public square splinters into social media silos.

The triumph of Trumpism was not the cause of this crisis of governance. It was a symptom of the decay of democratic institutions that, captured by the organized special interests of an insider establishment, failed to address the dislocations of globalization and the disruptions of rapid technological change. To add danger to decay, the fevered partisans of populism all too readily threw out the baby with the bathwater, assaulting the very integrity of institutional checks and balances that guarantee the enduring survival of republics. The revolt against a moribund political class transmuted into a revolt against governance itself.

Since neither the stakeholders of the old status quo nor the upstarts of populism have offered any effective, systemic solutions to what ails the nation, protracted polarization and paralysis set in.

In the end, there are only two solutions to this predicament — the move Trump has made toward strongman autocracy, or thinking outside the ballot box by inviting the broader civil society into governance through new mediating institutions of citizen engagement that complement representative government.

One reparative response, embryonic but indicative of the larger possibility, has been introduced in California: a first-in-the-nation online public platform to help bridge silos and mend the breach of distrust between the public and the institutions of self-government. The platform, called Engaged California (EC), encourages and facilitates the direct engagement of citizens with government and with each other.

Engaged California is not glorified polling and is more than a town hall gathering. It is a three-way tool that enables policymakers and administrators to listen at scale to average citizens outside of election cycles and be responsive; it invites citizens to directly voice their concerns and proposals on an ongoing basis; and it is a platform for Californians from all walks of life to interact with each other to find common ground.

AI serves as a sorting tool to register consensus among thousands of participants on priorities for government action and to collate fresh ideas that emerge from this practice of collective intelligence.

In short, it is exactly this kind of innovative institutional platform for “governing with the people” that can restore trust because the public itself is proactively engaged.

Beyond Tinkering

Since the great transformations underway in America today are systemic in nature, so too must new ways and means of governance go beyond tinkering around the edges of waning ways that no longer fit the times.

Governance is how communities invent and shape their destiny. It determines whether a society goes forward or backward. Like the homeostasis of all organisms, governance is the regulator, arbiter and navigator of human affairs. It processes emotions through reason, as the means by which societies not only survive but thrive by adapting to change.

Going forward in this light, democratic practices and institutions must adapt to the unprecedented scale of connectivity in a way that fosters a governing consensus instead of dividing the body politic against itself. In an AI economy, where massive new wealth is being generated by mining the general intellect of public data and transforming it into a productive asset, the old industrial division between labor and capital diminishes and everyone must become an owner sharing fairly in that wealth.

With the old slate now wiped clean by failed alternatives, the space is opening once again for the political imagination to think anew with a systemic response to the challenges at hand. The blue wave rebuke of Trumpism puts the onus on Democrats.

stories.body:
Battery maker CATL aims to have 2,000 swapping stations in China by the end of 2027 and to bring the tech to Europe

E very day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China . A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about.

“When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts.

Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery.

In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says.

Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total ) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy.

To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.”

This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling.

“Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says.

When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions.

It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT).

The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says.

The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries.

“If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says.

after newsletter promotion

CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs.

CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000.

The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035.

In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet. In 2024, about one-third of the zero-emission trucks in the country featured this technology, while the rest largely had conventional plug-in charging, according to the latest available figures .

One downside is that drivers often need to stick to a particular service provider that caters to the specific type of swappable batteries their e-trucks use.

“For example, some batteries are swapped from the chassis, while others are swapped from the top of the truck,” says Xue Lulu, a senior associate at World Resources Institute China. “Even under the same technological route, batteries made by different companies often have different specifications.” This means drivers cannot drop into any random swapping station to get their trucks replenished, which could restrict the journeys they can make, she says.

Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says. During her field research in China, she found some lorry drivers would wait outside battery-swapping stations for one to two hours before going in because they wanted to avoid using the service during peak hours, to save money. “Logistics firms are extremely sensitive to costs,” she says.

The most suitable users are probably drivers who, like Wang, work on fixed routes served by battery-swapping stations. Mao says the charging method has been rolled out most successfully among companies that use heavy trucks in specific settings, such as those carrying goods in ports and factories, as well as within a city or between two nearby cities. “For unpredicted and long-haul routes, there are still challenges for rolling it out on a large scale,” he says.

CEO says ‘democratic approach’ has helped brand outperform tough market, with big rises in China and US

Burberry has returned to profit as its back-to-basics strategy drove strong sales of the British brand’s coats, jackets and handbags over the summer.

Joshua Schulman, the chief executive, said the luxury brand had outperformed a “challenging luxury market” to achieve sales growth of 6%, helped by strong online and wholesale sales particularly in China and the US. “Our strategy is working,” he said.

Burberry said it made a pre-tax profit of £19m in the six months to 26 September after a loss of £48m a year before, as sales rose to £1.1bn. Sales rose 15% in China and 14% in the Americas but fell 1% in the Europe and Middle East region, partly due to the Iran war.

Schulman said Burberry’s focus on a “pyramid of pricing” ranging from more “affordable” scarves, starting from £195, and cotton-cashmere socks from £85, to its top-tier bags and coats, which can cost more than £9,000 for a leather version, had helped it achieve growth despite a tough market. Wealthy shoppers around the world are travelling less and being more cautious about spending, hitting luxury brand sales globally.

Sales of lightweight jackets and “tropical” gaberdine raincoats as well as its Cotswold range of leather bags and accessories featuring the brand’s famous check had proved popular.

Schulman said: “Luxury customers around the world are experiencing some fatigue with exorbitant pricing and in this context our strategy of having great value for money is resonating strongly with Chinese customers.”

“Burberry has always had a somewhat more democratic approach than some of our European peers and has a universal appeal,” he added.

Schulman said the brand had spent the last two years of its Burberry Forward strategy returning to its historical position at the “sweet spot in the luxury market”.

He said investment in locally relevant marketing, such as special product for China’s Valentine’s Day celebrations this spring and for the upcoming lunar new year, were also helping drive sales.

“It is no secret global tourism is down but the local customer has been spending in their respective regions,” Schulman said. “This is a trend we have been seeing all year long.”

While people were spending less as tourists which was hitting sales in discount outlets, Schulman said local spending was holding up in the brand’s flagship city centre stores including in London.

He said that while “nobody has a crystal ball” about whether customers would begin spending more freely, history suggested “this is a very cyclical business”.

stories.body:
Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy .

The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker’s board has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. The firm’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management.

Nvidia did not give a timeframe for the investigation but the company has said Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”. A committee of independent board directors, assisted by Kim and Wachtell, will oversee the investigation.

The company is reeling from an espionage scandal after reports that its chief executive had been having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was also an Nvidia customer.

The US ambassador to China , David Perdue, said: “The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent.

“National security is part of this economic conversation because economic security is national security. And so, what we’re doing with China is bumpy right now,” he told Bloomberg Television.

Nvidia had at first denied an improper relationship with the Chinese citizen, who is no relation to the Nvidia boss, but Huang then admitted on Sunday he had been unfaithful to his wife – without referring directly to Ms Huang.

On the same day Nvidia announced an investigation into reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.

The Wall Street Journal and the New York Times yesterday reported Huang had had another affair with an executive who reports to him, which led Nvidia stocks to fall by more than 8% in extended trading.

Shares had earlier staged a recovery on Wednesday, closing up 2.9% to $173.73 to narrow the market cap loss since Friday, before Huang admitted to the first marital infidelity, to $311bn. AI stocks were also lifted by results from CoreWeave, which jumped more than 24% after the AI infrastructure company reported strong revenue growth.

Wachtell is one of the most prestigious corporate law firms in the US. Its founding partner Martin Lipton invented the “poison pill defence” in the 1980s, a corporate gambit that helps companies ward off hostile takeovers.

Technically called the “shareholder rights plan”, the poison pill allowed investors to buy more shares at a discount if one shareholder acquired a certain percentage of the company’s stock. This made it harder for corporate raiders to acquire a company without the board’s approval.

The firm was closely involved in the takeover of Getty Oil by Texaco. This was the largest corporate takeover in history at the time, although it turned sour when the thwarted suitor Pennzoil sued Texaco and won.

In 2008, a team of Wachtell lawyers advised the US Treasury department on the takeover of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac during the financial crisis.

The company was founded in the 1960s and is said to be the most profitable law firm in the US. It pulled in revenues of $5.1m per lawyer last year and made profits of $12m per partner, the highest profits per partner ever, according to the Am Law 100 rankings .

after newsletter promotion

From 2017 to 2018, Kim was the acting US attorney for the southern district of New York, where he ran a team of lawyers investigating securities and commodities fraud, mail and wire fraud, public and private corruption, money laundering, cybercrime and tax offences.

That included the case of the former US representative Anthony Weiner , who was sentenced to 21 months in prison for sending obscene material to a minor.

He also oversaw the prosecution of the banker Mehmet Hakan Atilla, who was convicted in 2017 of helping to evade US sanctions on Iran .

Another high-profile assignment landed on Kim’s desk in 2021, when he investigated multiple allegations of sexual harassment by the then New York governor, Andrew Cuomo.

One analyst has put Huang’s chances of leaving Nvidia at 15%.

“Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the board investigation is completed,” wrote the tech analyst Dan Ives in a note to investors. “We would expect a board investigation that could take four weeks to six weeks and will create a clear overhang on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia.”

However after reports of the second extramarital affair, the WSJ last night reported that the board was preparing to oust Huang.

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and the founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, has put Huang’s survival chances at “about 50-50”.

stories.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
stories.summary: ﻿The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to September, according to official figures.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Computer programming and consultancy services in particular contributed to overall growth (generic photo)

Published 12 November 2026, 07:05 GMT

﻿The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures , external show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.

Although investors have recently been concerned about slower artificial intelligence development in the US and the long term viability of AI firms' business models, businesses have continued to invest in the technologies.

Sarah Coles, from investment platform AJ Bell, said that since the start of the year, "it's the less visible back-office work that has delivered, with administrative and supportive services seeing strong growth" noting that these are the areas benefitting from the increasing use of AI.

The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise".

A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said.

High energy costs have been stoked by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

US and Israeli attacks led to Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz - a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas.

Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other's oil refineries, leading to a squeeze on global refining capacity, hitting diesel and petrol prices.

What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you? Published 7 hours ago

'Surprising resilience'

Entrepreneur Richard Benc says the UK watch market and exports have been surprisingly resilient

Richard Benc, founder of mechanical watch company Studio Underdog, says sales are better than he expected.

"We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says.

The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers," he adds, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches.

stories.title: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
stories.summary: PM Andy Burnham was addressing delegates at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
PM Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to go to COP31

Published 5 hours ago

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".

Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.

But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.

In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.

Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.

He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office .

Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.

As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.

Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."

As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.

This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year.

The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.

Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.

"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.

Homes in the West Midlands were destroyed after record wildfires this summer in the UK

On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down.

He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity.

The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

Turkey, the co-hosts of COP31, wants a key outcomes of this year's summit to be a commitment by countries to meet 35% of their energy supply from electricity by 2035. Currently, it is around a fifth.

But Burnham has been accused of having double standards.

"The Prime Minister simply cannot call for clean power across the world while saying yes to more fossil fuels in the UK," said Beth John, climate adviser at Oxfam.

Last month, the government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on the grounds that it provided energy security.

And in the budget last month Chancellor John Healey announced a funding cut to the Warm Homes Plan, which provides grants and loans to support the installation of heat pumps.

Whilst this week there has been media speculation that the government is considering watering down electric car sales targets, although the government insists no decision has been made.

Successfully switching petrol and diesel cars to EVs and moving from gas boilers to electric-powered heat pumps are key ways to achieve the 35% electrification target , external .

Fire and Floods: Our Extreme Weather

The BBC's climate editor, Justin Rowlatt, investigates the impact of the changing climate on our weather.

Watch on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One (BBC Two in Northern Ireland) at 20:00 on Monday 9 November.

Although there was no royal presence this year, King Charles III sent a message ahead of Burnham's speech.

"As the world gathers for Cop31, I can only hope that this same spirit of partnership and common purpose can help inspire the collective action that our planet – and future generations – so urgently need.

"Our children and grandchildren will not judge us by the promises we made, but by what we chose to do."

Burnham was the only G7 leader to speak at this year's conference in a sign of faltering support for the COP process - something he acknowledged in his speech.

In an almost word for word copy of Sir Keir Starmer's address last year he said: "The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone, and the reality is now the world will reach 1.5 degrees."

Other leaders expected to speak on Thursday include many island states like Tonga, Tuvalu and the Solomon Islands.

For these nations, the impact of climate change is already at their front door. With most of their land just metres above sea level, rising water levels have caused many to abandon their homes in recent years.

Last year, Australia - the co-host of the COP31 summit - opened up the world's first climate visa for Tuvalu citizens wanting to evacuate.

The first intake was massively oversubscribed, with more than a third of the population entering the ballot.

As glaciers continue to melt and oceans expand, average sea levels are expected to keep climbing and potentially accelerate. The World Meteorological Organisation said on the opening day of this conference the global mean sea level was at its highest level since records began.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Manufacturer says ‘shift to new energy vehicles is happening faster than expected’ and market is harsh

The Japanese carmaker Nissan has said it has been caught out by accelerating sales of electric and hybrid cars in China amid a brutal price war in the world’s biggest automotive market.

The manufacturer slashed its sales forecasts for China and said it would cut back on petrol car manufacturing while increasing production of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, which combine a smaller battery with a petrol engine.

Nissan said it expected to sell between 2.97m and 3m cars this year, down from a previous forecast of 3.15m, mainly because of struggles in China.

“China remains our biggest challenge,” said Ivan Espinosa, Nissan’s chief executive. “Demand is weaker, competition is intensifying, and the shift to new energy vehicles is happening faster than expected. The market is being very, very harsh.”

The company reported increased sales in its home market as well as in North America, regions in which the shift to electric cars has been much slower because of policy decisions, including Donald Trump’s tearing up of incentives for battery car makers.

That divergence between different parts of the world illustrates the challenge for global carmakers, many of whom are trying to continue selling their more profitable petrol and diesel cars for as long as possible while risking being left behind by newer Chinese rivals .

China’s government gave weighty subsidies to its electric car industry, spotting an opportunity to overtake other countries such as Germany, Japan and the US, which had dominated sales of internal combustion engine cars.

That led to a huge number of Chinese EV competitors, which are now chasing a shrinking market. Nissan said sales across China fell by 22% in the first half of the year. That pressure “intensified from July through October” and left the carmaker’s sales down 32% in the first nine months of the year, Nissan said.

Espinosa said Nissan’s product lineup in China, led by the Sylphy family of saloon cars, was too heavily associated with petrol engines, so the company was cutting local production, exporting some products, while trying to ramp up its N series of models, which are electric or plug-in hybrids.

Yet at the same time as pushing for increased electric car production in China, Nissan has been among the manufacturers slowing the shift to batteries in Europe. In the UK the carmaker has lobbied to weaken the zero-emission vehicle mandate , a target for increasing EV sales, and to continue to sell petrol cars after 2035 .

after newsletter promotion

That lobbying came despite evidence of rising demand for electric cars in the UK, particularly since the Iran war pushed up petrol and diesel prices. Data this week showed that sales of used electric vehicles rose much faster than petrol cars.

Ian Plummer, the chief customer officer at the car sales website Autotrader, said: “The standout trend in the used car market is the rapid rise of retail sales of electric vehicles, up an eye-popping 56% year on year in October and now accounting for one in 10 retail sales on Autotrader.”

Nissan’s only European factory is in Sunderland in northern England. Espinosa said he was hopeful that the company’s products from Sunderland and Japan would be included in proposed “Made in Europe” rules from the EU . The rules as drafted would exclude all of Nissan’s cars from subsidies and other incentives within the EU, adding to pressure on the carmaker.

stories.title: Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others
stories.summary: Ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc, the prime minister's stance on Europe is causing MPs to think about their leaders' individual strategy.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 12 November 2026, 00:30 GMT

There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others.

Andy Burnham told his Cabinet earlier this week: "I firmly believe we have ended up with a harder Brexit than people voted for… no sensible person thinks the deal negotiated by the Tories is working for the country."

It comes ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc. On Thursday, at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Burnham will for the first time meet those who could prove pivotal as he sells his vision for Britain's future in the bloc.

And next week, he will deliver a speech on foreign policy, in which – for Burnham – Europe is a central plank. He will then travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility.

Talking about the new deal to be signed at the summit, Burnham said to ministers: "We will take opportunities that make people in this country better off.

"There is a significant prize."

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September

UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports Published 3 November

This lies behind the prime minister's decision to open the door to the argument about rejoining the EU single market - along with the freedom of movement that would bring - and even the EU altogether.

But that longer-term ambition is dividing his cabinet and his party.

Some welcome his approach, including those with formerly Brexit-backing constituencies. Angela Rayner, for example, is understood to have been pushing former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to be bolder on Brexit since at least autumn 2022.

The housing secretary is said to have been insistent that Labour needs to stick to its manifesto red lines – not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement – but is open minded to changing those at the next election.

Another cabinet minister said: "The best thing you can do in politics is tell the truth. And the truth is that Brexit has been hugely damaging to Britain.

"We are not leading a public conversation here, we are racing to catch up with the public."

But others are watching nervously at a strategy one former minister described as "high risk".

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, for example, has struck a more cautious tone warning about the "costs and consequences" of rejoining the EU as well as staying out.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business and Trade Secretary, is supportive of getting closer to the EU and discussing the UK's long term relationship.

But he has previously warned against joining the EU's customs union and is also unsure about the prospect of rejoining the EU, highlighting the uncertainty of what terms the UK would face, and what the bloc could look like in years to come with nationalist parties in the ascendancy in several European countries.

A voice from the past has a different set of concerns.

Lord Cameron told Bloomberg's Mishal Husain that starting a conversation about rejoining would be "very long and painful".

The former prime minister warned "flirting with rejoining" could also harm Burnham's attempts to renegotiate the Conservative's Brexit deal.

"If you start endlessly producing this idea that we're actually on a path to rejoining, I think you're in danger of getting a less good partnership deal because of course the EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."

Attitudes in Labour towards the prime minister's approach don't divide along predictable lines. One Scottish Labour MP, personally opposed to Brexit and with a heavily Remain-voting constituency, said it was a "real problem".

"How can I argue to my constituents that we had a Scottish referendum in 2014 that settled independence for a generation. but then say the 2016 referendum isn't settled? My view is you accept democracy."

For now though, that opposition hasn't broken out into public rebellion, although Labour MP Gareth Snell is one who has warned about reopening the debate.

The MP for Stoke-on-Trent, where the Leave vote was 69.4%, told the BBC's Westminster Hour that doing so would "monopolise an awful lot of time inside parliament, inside government" when there are other things MPs should be doing.

Two Labour MPs among those most unhappy about Burnham's openness to Europe insisted "there are no plans" for any organised criticism of the prime minister.

Despite their concerns, particularly about free movement, they described their current mindset as "wait and see". That temporary truce is likely to fracture if the prime minister's lead in the polls begins to slide.

Badenoch has pledged that a future Conservative government will withdraw the UK from the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)

But Burnham's strategy has left other parties struggling to react.

The Conservatives have strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules into the future, with the party leader Kemi Badenoch saying that would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".

But some Conservative MPs are beginning to express unease about the strategic dilemma presented for their party by Burnham's moves on Europe, fearing that the issue could again divide Conservative voters.

In recent months Badenoch and her team have intensified efforts to win back affluent voters, especially in the south of England, who view Burnham's economic offer as too left-wing.

"The problem is that some of those voters are only just giving us a hearing again after Brexit," one Conservative MP said, "and now they are going to keep being reminded of it."

The Liberal Democrats have enjoyed being the most pro-European of the largest parties in Westminster. But some Lib Dems now fear their distinct position risks being drowned out by Burnham.

Reform UK though say they are "very bullish" about the return of Brexit to political debate, despite polling that suggests public sentiment has shifted since 2016.

"If he [Burnham] wants to fight an election on a £40bn bill to rejoin, open door immigration, and less control over our laws and our courts then we are very up for that," a Reform UK strategist said.

The party believes that just as it would build a progressive anti-Brexit coalition around Labour, it would also unite Brexit supporters around Reform UK as the most anti-EU party.

stories.body:
Western military forces increasingly worried Chinese-made technology ⁠could send ‌sensitive information to Beijing

Germany has banned commercially available Chinese-made drones ⁠from its military bases and training grounds due to security concerns, ⁠according to reports.

Western military forces have grown increasingly concerned that Chinese-made technology ⁠could pose a security risk and may be ​used to transmit ‌sensitive information to Beijing.

Germany’s drone ban, effective immediately, follows the US military banning China’s BYD electric vehicles from its Kadena airbase on the Japanese island of Okinawa. Kadena, the biggest US air force base in east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .

The German newspaper Der Spiegel reported that the drones, ‌acquired by military units in recent years with limited bureaucratic oversight, are being withdrawn from service as quickly as possible. The defence ministry was not immediately available for comment.

Local commanders had been allowed to buy the drones under ‌a 2024 strategy that included a “white list” of approved systems, including several made by the ​China-based DJI, the world’s largest drone maker.

As there is no central record of purchases by individual units, the military has to ⁠impose a blanket ban, Der Spiegel reported.

In February, Poland barred Chinese-made vehicles from entering its military facilities over concerns that onboard sensors could be used to collect sensitive data.

The army said Chinese-made vehicles may still be allowed on to secured sites if specified functions are disabled and other safeguards required under each facility’s security rules are in place.

When the US military announced its ban on BYD vehicles entering Kadena airbase, Lt Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force, said: “These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission.”

American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.

In safety advice issued in September, the Dutch government said smart features built into modern vehicles – including microphones, cameras and GPS trackers – could be used by hostile states to spy on people . The warning from the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service did not mention countries or manufacturers by name.

That alert followed reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.

Last week, a group of MEPs urged the European Commission to assess whether BYD cars posed a security threat and should ​be subject to restrictions, such as excluding them from public procurement purchases.

after newsletter promotion

In written questions, 14 ​parliamentarians asked that the EU’s cybersecurity agency assess the level of threat ​and potentially include BYD on a list of high-risk suppliers.

François Kalfon, the ⁠French MEP leading the push, wrote in a preamble to the questions that China’s ​2017 national intelligence law required companies to cooperate with the state. “Allowing connected vehicles from third ​countries to access sensitive European infrastructure therefore poses an unacceptable security risk,” he wrote.

In a statement , BYD said no data processed or stored, whether in the cloud or within a vehicle, could be remotely accessed from China, ​and that customers remained in control of their data. “BYD Europe does not make such ​data available to BYD entities or third parties in China.”

In 2018, the US defence department banned the use of smartphones from the Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide, citing security concerns.

stories.title: 'Not the answer': Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
stories.summary: There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field will be given the green light.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through a large ship 80 miles north west of Shetland

Published 11 November 2026

Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.

There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective".

But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits.

Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports. Reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.

Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support.

One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate".

"The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said.

Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer.

Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test.

"It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices."

Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise."

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh . She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh will formally announce the Rosebank decision, expected in the coming weeks

Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields".

Licences for both Jackdaw and Rosebank were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 respectively.

But the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approvals unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a fresh decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch sought to tease at Labour divisions on the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday.

Demand for fossil fuels

During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails."

Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future".

She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency."

Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake.

"Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added.

Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Labour MP Bill Esterson, chair of Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, said "the economics of it (Rosebank) are that you should carry on with it" and "there's an element of energy security" by approving it.

Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either".

"This government will not make decisions for this country which are not compatible with our climate obligations," he added.
