stories.title: Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller
stories.summary: Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise , offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative. It’s essentially a portmanteau biopic: its hero is Cui Xun, a fictional stand-in for the venerable Cui Daozhi , a still-extant real-life figure who so revolutionised forensic science he became known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. Ripping three-and-a-bit tales from the casebook – involving a 1970s child killer, a grisly 1980s multiple murder and a 1990s bus bombing (plus one lingering loose end), Chen constructs a history of forensic investigation that is also, in variably oblique ways, a history of Chinese law enforcement, which is shown evolving from boozy, gloveless crime-scene trampling to something far more streamlined and professional. Within the handsome period framework, Chen follows the science: one era’s crazy innovation becomes commonplace in the next. A rookie Cui (played here by Zhang Yi, ageing up subtly) uses boiled potatoes to take dental imprints; when these run out, he and his colleagues start biting one another’s cheeks to make their points. By the 90s, when Cui is heading a team working out of a vast, well-staffed warehouse, we seem mere moments away from David Caruso’s sunglasses and memorable Who guitar riffs. stories.title: Burnham signals backing for more ethnicity options on next census
stories.summary: It comes after a Lib Dem MP said black English or Asian English should be specific options for respondents.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 11 November 2026

Andy Burnham has signalled his support for dedicated options at the next census to allow people to define themselves as black English or Asian English.

It comes after Liberal Democrat MP Josh Babarinde called for legislation to widen ethnicity options for respondents at the next population count, due in 2031.

The last census, held in 2021, saw English offered within a broader white category, but without specific options for black English or Asian English.

Asked at Prime Minister's Questions whether he would support Babarinde's proposal, Burnham said he had not seen details of the plan.

But he added: "I stand here thinking that I would want to support that bill, to directly take on the poisonous politics we've seen from some in this House".

"We must bring people back together. I am interested in working with anyone in this House who shares that aim," he added.

Burnham did not respond to a follow-up question from Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey about whether he would meet Babarinde to discuss his plan, and he did not specify whether the government would give it time for debate in Parliament.

Babarinde introduced his proposal for legislation on Tuesday, under a rule that allows MPs to propose new laws in a 10-minute speech.

Such draft laws, known as private members' bills, rarely become law without support from the government of the day but are often used by MPs to raise awareness of issues and generate media attention for policy ideas.

Census should include black English and Asian English options, says MP Published 1 day ago

Respondents to the 2021 census were asked a two-stage question about ethnicity, with options grouped under five broad ethnic headings.

In Wales, the terms "Asian Welsh" and "Black Welsh" were listed in the broad categories themselves, and respondents were able to pick "Welsh" as an option underneath the broader white category.

The form in England listed "English" as an option in the white ethnic category, but the only way for respondents to describe themselves as Black English or Black English was via a free-form text box.

In Scotland, the term "Scottish Asian" appeared in the broad categories, whilst "Black Scottish" was given as an example response for the text box.

Speaking on Tuesday, Babarinde said his proposed law would introduce Black English and Asian English as specific new categories, arguing that the text box on the current form "may as well be the margin".

Braverman 'Englishness' remarks

Babarinde's proposal has been backed by some MPs in other parties, including Labour former deputy prime minister David Lammy and Conservative Sir James Cleverly, who quit the shadow cabinet this summer to run for London mayor.

The Eastbourne MP has previously told the BBC he put forward his bill in the wake of comments by former Conservative home secretary Suella Braverman, who defected to Reform UK earlier this year.

Braverman wrote in 2015 , external that she was British Asian but said she "cannot claim to be English" despite being born and educated in England.

She has reaffirmed her position in recent weeks, writing on X that Englishness was "an ethnicity" and it was "not racist to say this".

"To say I'm English is to take a 'laissez-faire, anything-goes' attitude to ethnicity, citizenship and identity. It also denies me my Asian heritage," she added.

The detailed questions asked during the census in England and Wales are set out in legislation following recommendations from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The ONS told the BBC that the Government Statistical Service has been working on a new approach to asking about ethnicity in official surveys since 2022, with an update on the work due to be published on Thursday.

That could lead to a recommendation to change the ethnicity question at the 2031 census, although the questionnaire itself is normally designed much closer to the time the census is due to take place.

Legislation setting out the questions for the last census was published in summer 2020, ahead of it taking place in March the following year.

The Scottish government delayed the census in Scotland until 2022 because of the Covid pandemic.

stories.title: Former minister calls for phone tech to block live-streamed child sex abuse
stories.summary: New technology would block the live-streaming of child sexual abuse on phones, tablets and laptops.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The UK is one of the three biggest markets for live streamed child sexual abuse in the world

Published 11 November 2026

Former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips has joined calls from campaigners for the government to back new technology that blocks the live-streaming of child sexual abuse.

The UK National Crime Agency has flagged the UK as the third biggest market in the world , external for live-streamed abuse, where children are sexually abused live on camera to order.

Device-level blockers can prevent this material being filmed and viewed on smartphones, laptops and tablets in the first place, Phillips said, at the launch of a policy report in Parliament.

Anti-abuse campaigners claim keeping the technology at device level maintains privacy and encryption. Civil liberties campaigners Big Brother Watch dispute this.

The government has already legislated to demand tech firms like Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, block under-18s from taking or sharing nude images on smartphones and other devices.

However, three-quarters of child sexual abuse material (CSA) was not self-generated but likely captured on adult devices, according to 2025 research from the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), which works to eliminate child sexual abuse imagery online.

Some 1.8 million men in the UK admitted to some form of online sexual offending against children, according to research from child safety institute Childlight.

Phillips, who complained of repeated delays to work to tackle CSA when she resigned as safeguarding minister in May, is demanding action to tackle the source of the crime and reduce the number of British offenders.

"This should be a source of national shame, and we must stop it," the Labour MP said.

"The technology, the evidence and the public support are all there - I want to work with ministers to extend on-device blocking to child sexual abuse material on every device sold in Britain, making children here and over the world safer."

The software uses AI to classify known child abuse images in the phone's operating system, and blocks the material at the moment it is viewed or created, whatever app is in use.

Nothing is logged, stored or sent anywhere, and the tech would work alongside encryption.

The AI classifier has been trained against a database of known child abuse images so it can differentiate between harmless material such as children at the beach, and sexual abuse.

Phillips said online child sexual abuse is "an issue that we did not keep control of" as legislators and now must be prioritised, at the event in Parliament.

She was joined by survivors of online child sexual abuse, who said they should not have to beg for the removal of images of themselves being abused from the internet.

Phil Eccles, from the National Crime Agency (NCA), said the scale of the problem was "at crisis point".

"This would cut off at source somebody on the UK their ability to direct a live stream for a child to be abused," he said.

"To me, safeguarding children will always supersede the ability to prosecute. If we can stop that abuse we must.

"But it's so important that tech companies come onboard - we cannot arrest our way out of this problem."

New law to force tech firms to stop children taking or sharing nude images Published 8 September

What the Online Safety Act is - and how to keep children safe online Published 24 July 2025

UK police bosses say unsafe social media platforms should be blocked for under-16s Published 22 May

The parliamentary briefing also heard from the former minister, Conservative Lord Nash, who led the campaign for an under-16s social media ban.

He said: "By the time the police are involved, a child has already been abused and the images and videos have gone round the globe.

"The material has to be blocked on the phone itself, before the harm is done.

"The government deserves real credit for committing to exactly that on children's phones.

"I urge it now to extend that commitment to every device sold in Britain, targeted at CSA material, and to lead the world in doing so."

In a sign of CSA becoming more prevalent, communications watchdog Ofcom has found almost as many offenders looking for CSA on everyday apps on the open web as on the dark web.

John Tanagho, from the anti-trafficking organisation the International Justice Mission, highlighted how children in poorer countries were being targeted for sexual exploitation, with research showing one in every 100 Filipino children were victims.

Legislation should explicitly limit the scans to identifying and blocking CSA material, he said, with no data shared with the government or any private companies, maintaining privacy.

However, civil liberties campaigners Big Brother Watch warned about the possibility of innocent images being blocked or the technology being adapted for surveillance in future.

"Effective child protection requires a stronger criminal justice response," a spokesperson said.

"Yet police are already overwhelmed by reports of child sexual abuse, while the NCA has rightly raised concerns that eight in ten offenders convicted of possessing child abuse images avoid prison.

"Genuine child protection requires well-resourced, targeted policing and robust enforcement of the law, not the scanning of every phone in Britain."

A government spokesperson did not respond directly to the new call for CSA blockers, but said: "We are putting in place the strongest online safety laws in the world.

"This includes preparing world-first legislation to call on the biggest technology companies to make it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images.

"We will also give the police the powers they need to keep pace with criminal use of emerging technologies in order to keep our children safe."

stories.body:
Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’

Cop31 live – latest updates

China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels , and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.

As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.

In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.

Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.

Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”

For autocratic states without free and fair elections , seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.

“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”

He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”

China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.

Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way : “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”

China as a ‘doer and go-getter’

The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows .

Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.

The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.

after newsletter promotion

“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”

Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed .

Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.

The need for trust

China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.

Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”

If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.

Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.

They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.

For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”

stories.title: Reform boycotts Senedd after member banned for saying white people are being replaced
stories.summary: Party members withdrew from most of Wednesday's Senedd proceedings over Joe Martin's speaking ban.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reform UK Wales member Joe Martin, party leader Helen Jenner and chief whip Llŷr Powell announced the boycott on the Senedd's steps

Published 11 November 2026

Reform UK have partially boycotted the Senedd in protest against a ban on one of their politicians for claiming white people are being "replaced".

The party's Welsh leader, Helen Jenner, said Joe Martin's ban was because of "undue pressure" from governing party Plaid Cymru and was an "infringement on freedom of speech".

Martin had been told he would not be allowed to speak in the Senedd's chamber until he apologised for the remarks, which the parliament's Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called the ruling "ridiculous and outrageous".

Reform members, who make up by far the Senedd's largest opposition party, withdrew from most of the day's proceedings but returned to vote in the parliament in the evening.

Joe Martin was told he would not be called to speak until he apologised

Jenner confirmed her party's boycott on the steps of the Senedd on Wednesday afternoon.

"It is now clear that the freedom of speech of one of our Senedd members is being curtailed, meaning his constituents are being silenced," she said.

"We stand behind Joe, and we will not attend today's plenary session in protest at his treatment.

"Every Reform MS [ Member of the Senedd ] will be in their Senedd office working hard for our constituents."

Martin said he would not apologise.

"My voters sent me to the Senedd to speak on their behalf," he said.

"I am being blocked from doing so, and now it's clear that I have fewer rights than the people who elected me.

"That cannot be the situation in a national parliament."

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Why has a Reform MS been banned from speaking in the Senedd?

Asked by BBC Wales if he genuinely believed white people were being "replaced" in the UK, Martin said: "That's obviously a fact."

Aliya Mohammed, chief executive of the charity Race Equality First, said "the idea that white people are being 'replaced' is linked to a conspiracy theory that creates division and wrongly portrays people from minority ethnic backgrounds as a threat".

"Immigration can and should be debated, but language that fuels fear and hostility has no place in public discourse," she said.

"Being Welsh or British is not defined by race or skin colour.

"Wales belongs to all of us, and our diversity is one of our greatest strengths."

Posting on X, Farage said it was "ridiculous and outrageous that Reform's duly elected Member of the Senedd, Joe Martin, has been banned from speaking in the Welsh Parliament".

"Why is it only Reform that's targeted like this?" he asked.

Martin was also backed by the leader of right-wing party Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe.

He called for the Senedd to be "shut down" if it was "going to shut down legitimate debate around demographic security and immigration".

Martin's Caerdydd Penarth constituency includes some of Wales' most ethnically diverse communities.

Farage announced Jenner as his party's Welsh leader at the Senedd in September

On Tuesday Martin asked for a Welsh government statement on the "demographic replacement of white British people" during business questions, when Senedd members are free to raise issues they choose.

Business Minister Heledd Fychan immediately asked the presiding officer whether the remarks were within the Senedd's standing orders - a set of rules that govern conduct in the chamber.

Standing orders give the presiding officer discretion to decide if contributions to plenary sessions - meetings of the full Senedd - use "discriminatory or offensive language".

Delivering his ruling later, Irranca-Davies said: "Until I receive a clear indication that the member understands the boundaries of acceptable parliamentary conduct and apologises to the Siambr [chamber], we will not be calling him to speak."

Senedd officials confirmed an apology would have to be made in the chamber during a plenary session.

The ruling does not cover committees.

Martin is a member of the Senedd's Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee.

Irranca-Davies pointed out it was not the first time he had rebuked Martin. In September, he said Martin had made offensive remarks about surgeons working in the Welsh NHS gender service .

Plaid Cymru Senedd member Carrie Harper called Reform's boycott a "pathetic tantrum" that was a "disgrace to democracy".

"They'd rather play gimmicks and chase headlines than be serious about Wales' future and doing the job they were elected to do on behalf of the people they represent," she said.

Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates said he was "astonished" that Reform had "chosen Remembrance Day of all days to pull a political stunt".

"They claim to be on the side of our armed forces, of our veterans, yet when they have the chance to speak up on behalf of this community, they bolt," he said.

"It is shameful, unpatriotic and disrespectful to the Armed Forces community."

In the 2021 census 93.8% of people in Wales identified as white, down from 95.6% a decade earlier, with the country's overall population growing by 1.4% to 3,107,500.

The proportion identifying as Asian, Asian Welsh or Asian British, the next highest group in the survey, rose from 2.3% to 2.9%.

Mixed or multiple ethnic groups rose from 1% to 1.6%, and those identifying as Black, Black Welsh, Black British, Caribbean or African rose from 0.6% to 0.9%.

Thinktank Niesr says timid rate rise last week likely to make inflation more persistent feature of UK economy

The Bank of England is risking higher interest rates for longer after a hesitant response to rising inflation , according to leading thinktank.

In a searing critique of the central bank’s tactics, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) said a timid increase in interest rates last week was likely to mean inflation staying above the Bank’s 2% target until at least 2030.

The thinktank said inflation was likely to become a more persistent feature of the UK economy unless the Bank took tougher action .

The Bank’s monetary policy committee increased the cost of borrowing from 3.75% to 4% last week and hinted at another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

The director of the Niesr, David Aikman, urged the Bank of England to be more aggressive in tackling inflation, saying all the ingredients were in place for workers to demand inflation-linked salary rises.

“Inflation is set to rise above 4% in the new year, just as most pay awards for 2027 are being agreed, so the risk that it becomes embedded is rising.

“One further quarter-point rise is unlikely to be enough, and the longer the MPC waits, the more it will eventually need to do.”

UK inflation stands at 3.5%, well above the Bank’s 2% target, driven higher by the soaring cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have risen sharply since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.

Brent crude oil has persistently traded at more than $100 a barrel in recent weeks – compared with about $70 before the war – but on Tuesday it traded below $90 at one point, the lowest since 31 August, after Donald Trump downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”.

Investors, however, reined in their enthusiasm after US inflation climbed by 0.4 percentage points from September to October , revealing that high oil and gas prices were continuing to drive up costs. The S&P 500 index of leading US companies was down 0.9% by early afternoon on Wall Street.

The Niesr said its forecasts for growth in the UK and the global economy were based on oil prices at $105 a barrel. However, it cautioned that while prices had dropped, continued difficulties shipping and refining meant consumer prices would decline slowly.

Stephen Millard, an economist at the institute, said the lower oil price was also dependent on Trump sticking to his new policy. “We’ve seen him change his mind before,” he said.

The chancellor, John Healey, was criticised for deferring difficult decisions in the budget last month, which the institute said would leave a £30bn hole in the government’s finances if the pattern of doing so over the last decade was repeated next year.

Aikman said financial markets would punish the Treasury by raising the price of loans to the UK if it became clear that government spending was going to soar in areas such as defence without savings being made elsewhere.

He said there was a “double whammy” from higher energy prices and rising global borrowing costs that was not being addressed.

Closing summary

Shares of Nvidia tumbled 5% on Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Nvidia’s announcement of the investigation on Sunday came after its boss admitted that he had an affair with Alice Huang , an executive at Singapore-based datacenter company Megaspeed, who according to the New York Times , US intelligence determined was gathering information for China. The episode has thrown Jensen Huang’s future at the company – and that of Nvidia itself – up in the air, and raises serious questions about US national security – given Jensen Huang’s close relationship with Donald Trump – and what Alice Huang could have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair.

The New York Times reported in ​October that Trump was briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing, but the US president did not act on it. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I have not ​spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.” Trump later added: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.” He said he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.

The New York Times also reported on Monday that a US commerce department investigation into Megaspeed – the data company led by Alice Huang – was halted after Nvidia’s general counsel intervened. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, reportedly contacted the investigators at commerce department to inform them that their boss, Jeff Kessler – a top official – had given Teter permission to request details about their probe into Megaspeed. The case focused on whether the company was smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China. According to current and former government officials, and others familiar with the incident, that the NYT spoke to, some viewed Kessler’s interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the investigation. The case was eventually transferred to the US justice department late last year, but questions remain about Kessler’s discussions with Nvidia, and what information he subsequently relayed to Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary or the wider Trump administration. According to the Times’ sources, the justice department is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed.

US Republican lawmakers expressed alarm over the episode, asking Jensen Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, currently the House minority leader who is poised to become new Speaker next year, said that he ‌wants restrictions on chips sales to China that in a Senate bill to ‌become law as part of ​an annual defence bill. “Clearly Congress needs more information,” about what ⁠happened at Nvidia, ​Jeffries said, ​adding ​that there are “real ​concerns ‌that ​need ​to be addressed with respect to the Nvidia situation.”

Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls, meanwhile, expressed their support for the embattled Nvidia CEO. Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. Maguire argued the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”. “Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted. “Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post. Bill Ackman , the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair. Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.

There’s a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post, wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives + Co., saying that Huang is “not replaceable.” “On the heels of last week’s Blue Tidal Wave this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China,” Ives wrote.

The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information. “The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

Briefing.com analyst Patrick O’Hare said that Nvidia was being treated as a one-off story by investors for the moment. “In other words, the stock is being penalised for Jensen Huang’s personal transgression, which has invited a great deal of uncertainty into the mix, but the market isn’t caught up in the notion that this situation is going to have a systemic domino effect,” he said.

The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month. A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

Over in the US Congress, Hakeem Jeffries , currently the House minority leader who is poised to become its new Speaker next year, has said ⁠that Congress ⁠needs answers after reports emerged ⁠ Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted ⁠by a foreign ​intelligence ‌effort.

Jeffries ‌also said he ‌wants restrictions on chips sales to China that in a Senate bill to ‌become law as part of ​an annual defence bill.

“ Clearly Congress needs more information ,” about what ⁠happened at Nvidia, ​Jeffries said, ​adding ​that there are “real ​concerns ‌that ​need ​to be addressed with respect to the Nvidia situation. ”

The AI poster boy, the ‘Chinese spy’ and Trump: how an affair may have harmed US security

Aisha Down and Dan Milmo

Reports that the boss of a cornerstone company in the global AI boom has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort are a big deal, given Jensen Huang ’s close relationship with the US president.

Aside from Jensen Huang’s dented personal reputation after admitting to having an affair with Alice Huang – an alleged Chinese spy - what is the scale of the damage done to Nvidia and US national security?

The story started to emerge last year when the New York Times and Bloomberg raised questions about a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia’s powerful chips. There were concerns that Megaspeed was flouting US restrictions on AI chip exports to China by diverting some Nvidia inventory to America’s arch AI rival. Nvidia and Megaspeed denied this.

Then last month came a further startling NYT report that Jensen Huang, a Megaspeed executive, had formed a “close relationship” with Ms Huang and that American officials believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Donald Trump had been told, but decided not to act on the information. It is now evident that the relationship was more than just close.

At the heart of the question of what China might have achieved through Alice Huang is the extremely close relationship between the CEO of the world’s second-most-valuable company and the president of the United States.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia appeared to have successfully leaned on the US commerce department to halt an investigation into potential chip smuggling on the part of Megaspeed . That pressure came through a Trump appointee, who allowed Nvidia to reach out about the case.

Further, Trump has met frequently – at least seven times – with the head of Nvidia since the start of his second term. Huang has flown on Air Force One and taken calls from the president during public events.

Four of their meetings have touched on one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relationships : the controls that the US has put up around the export of the world’s most advanced AI chips, which are almost entirely sold by Nvidia.

The US president first invited Huang to the White House just six days after he was inaugurated, to discuss AI policy and chip exports . The two then met again in July and August of 2025. This was followed by victories for Huang – Trump allowed Nvidia to export previously banned chips to China. Nvidia agreed, in turn, to give the US government 15% of the sales revenue.

Five months later, the tech boss appeared to win another startling concession, days after another meeting with Trump. The president agreed to allow the tech boss to export H200s – a far more powerful chip – to China, in exchange for 25% of the revenue.

It is not unusual for large technology companies to lobby for their preferred policies in Washington; nor is it unusual for Trump to give access – and favourable deals – to men he likes.

But one more thing is now apparent – during this crucial year for his company, Huang was also intimately involved with a reported Chinese spy. The two were first photographed together in mid-2024. Five months after Trump took office is when the two were filmed at the Taipei restaurant. This would have been at the height of Huang’s lobbying push, shortly before Trump agreed to let Nvidia sell the H200s.

What could Alice Huang have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair? Plenty. Glimpses into US policy as it was being made, and to Trump’s own chaotic thinking on AI. And perhaps a world of tips beyond the confines of the White House.

Huang was a key figure for government after government as they formulated their AI policy. He met world leaders from South Korea to Saudi Arabia that year; he joined the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, on stage in London.

He would have known the details of the most important tech policy for many governments on Earth – their AI ambitions – because his company was often the only one that could make these ambitions happen. That is certainly true for Britain.

For all the intellectual feats of the systems powered by Nvidia technology, it is Huang’s human intelligence that is most valuable to America’s competitors.

As we’ve been reporting, shares of Nvidia tumbled more than 5% on Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang , was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Further to my last post regarding succession at Nvidia, there’s a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives + Co., told the Associated Press that Huang is “not replaceable”.

“On the heels of last week’s Blue Tidal Wave [in the US midterm elections] this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China,” Ives said.

Still, Ives said there is a risk, as Huang could be removed as CEO depending on the board’s investigation and that it will remain an overhang on shares near term.

Opinion: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish

Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang , the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal . The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.

Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.

There isn’t even a Nvidia board member with the title of chair. Instead, a “lead director” is “designated annually by a majority of the independent directors”, which sounds like a formula for ensuring the attention remains wholly focused on Huang, the sole executive member.

It’s the American way, of course: the cult of the superstar founder or chief executive runs deep and there is a fair argument that such set-ups encourage adventurous risk-taking in pursuit of grand corporate visions. But such governance arrangements look unsuited to situations where the behaviour of the boss is under scrutiny and the role of the board itself is being examined .

The investigation will examine whether Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort” but the independent directors stressed there is now “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

But legitimate questions don’t end there. Did Huang break Nvidia’s internal code of conduct ? Did he mislead the board about his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy? Was the board aware of US intelligence reports that Ms Huang had been hired by China’s ministry of state security to spy on the Nvidia boss, as reported by the New York Times? What security precautions were in place? Other boards in other countries might have insisted on suspending the boss until all the facts are in.

In the meantime, the defence of Huang from elsewhere has begun. “An honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” said Donald Trump . “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” opined Shaun Maguire , a partner at Sequoia Capital, the powerful Silicon Valley investor. Yes, there is little doubt the US tech and political establishment would like this saga to end up in a series of bland conclusions about an everyday infidelity.

Nvidia’s board, however, would be wise not to rely on the “irreplaceable” consensus holding, or the political heat going away. This affair will be trawled over by newly empowered Democrats in Congress because it touches on how forcefully – or not – the administration has been enforcing its own national security restrictions on chip sales to China. This process will go on for months. Huang’s personal relationship with Trump will come under the spotlight like never before.

Will the Nvidia boss, even if he is cleared by the board’s investigation, still look so all-conquering by the end? His lobbying clout in Washington will be diminished. And Nvidia’s shareholders, if they’re doing the job properly, will surely insist on far greater visibility on where the company’s chips end up.

There may come a point where it is in Nvidia’s own interests to move on from the Jensen Huang era. The 63-year-old deserves all his accolades for spotting the enormous AI opportunity for the GPU chips that originated in the world of video games. The rise of Nvidia has been extraordinary. But over-reliance on one individual is also a business risk. Time for some overdue succession planning – it may be needed.

Nvidia ’s embattled CEO Jensen Huang has disappeared from the line-up of two tech events he was due to speak at this week, according to Business Insider (paywall) .

Insider reports: “Ahead of its expected IPO next week, Anthropic is hosting a private CEO forum this week in Montecito. Huang was set to be interviewed by an Anthropic executive on Monday evening, a person familiar with the event told Business Insider. He is no longer expected to attend, according to a second person familiar with the matter.”

Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?

There is little public information available about Alice Huang , the woman reportedly at the centre of the Jensen Huang honeypot allegations , a fact that has only added fuel to claims she is a Chinese intelligence asset.

She was the chief executive of a Singapore-based datacentre company reportedly suspected of evading US export controls and routing Nvidia chips to China.

US officials then came to believe she was also a spy for Beijing who was having an affair with Jensen Huang , the chief executive of Nvidia, the chip company critical to US ambitions to stay ahead of China in the AI race.

People briefed on the US intelligence told the New York Times they believed Alice Huang was recruited as part of efforts to learn more about American AI chips, and to try to persuade Nvidia to push for its advanced chips to be made available to China.

China has denied the allegations, calling them “nothing but smears”.

It is unclear exactly when the two Huangs, who are not related, first met.

Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected within the upper echelons of the global AI chip industry, the New York Times wrote, citing people who had met her.

Megaspeed , the datacentre company for which she was previously listed as chief executive, still describes itself as “a premier business partner of Nvidia” on LinkedIn.

It was in this capacity that the businesswoman was pictured in Jensen Huang’s company several times in 2024 and 2025.

One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted by another attending company on LinkedIn, shows the two sitting next to each other on a couch in Taipei.

The year after, they were filmed together again in Taipei at a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

Press outside livestreamed footage of the two, seemingly comfortable in each other’s company, with Jensen Huang at one point putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kissed him on the cheek.

The two later left the restaurant in the same car, the footage showed.

A New York-based short-selling firm first raised concerns publicly about their “uncomfortably close relationship” six months ago.

Earlier this year, US officials wrote a memo saying the two Huangs had been romantically involved, the Financial Times reported on Saturday, citing sources who had seen it.

On Sunday the Nvidia chief executive sent a company-wide email apologising for an affair.

He did not name Alice Huang but said he would cooperate with an investigation “regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports”.

Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unknown, and she has not given a public statement about the allegations.

It is unclear what her current relationship is with Megaspeed, though Culper Research, the short-selling firm, quoted an employee in May as saying that contrary to public reporting, Alice Huang was “actually still our boss”.

The details of her career before that are difficult to ascertain.

Several media outlets have cited a profile matching her name and picture on a Chinese fund database, which listed previous jobs at banks including HSBC and CITIC, as well as roles at Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.

However, reporters have been unable to confirm any of the details listed.

Megaspeed is among a number of south-east Asian firms that buy chips to build facilities and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

According to Singapore’s the Straits Times, it was previously known as 7Road International – a Chinese gaming company with ties to state-backed investors.

At the time of the rebrand, it was owned by Huang Le Limited and led by Alice Huang, the newspaper said, before the ownership was transferred to another company in 2023.

Since late 2024, the US government has reportedly been investigating Megaspeed for helping companies in China sidestep American export restrictions.

The New York Times said Singapore questioned Alice Huang during its own investigation into the company, but released her.

Nvidia has previously said it has looked into Megaspeed but found no cause for concern.

The Guardian has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

XPeng says its $300k low-altitude device will soon be ready for emergency services and recreational use in rural areas

People could start taking trips in so-called flying cars in China as soon as next summer, the manufacturer of a two-seater vehicle with autopilot model has said.

Deli Zhao, the chief executive of the Chinese flying car company XPeng, said the $300,000 (£225,000) low-altitude device would be ready for use by recreational users in rural locations and by emergency services in the second half of 2027. After 10 years of development including trials of flying motorbikes at the company’s Guangzhou base, it has been approved by China’s civil aviation authorities for limited use.

The small cockpit is about the size of a Fiat 500 car and the vehicle is lifted into the air by six drone-like battery-powered propellers and steered by a simple joystick. It can also fly autonomously to a programmed destination, but Xhao, a trained pilot, claimed he could teach anyone to fly it in five minutes.

The price tag for the contraption includes a six-wheel van about the size of a Ford Transit, out of the back of which the flying vehicle unfolds “just like the Transformers”, said Zhao. He has been developing flying cars for almost a decade and said he was part-inspired by the flying creatures ridden by humans in the Harry Potter stories and the Green Goblin’s flying skateboard from the Spider-Man comics.

“The world where everyone can be a captain is about to arrive,” he said at the Web Summit in Lisbon on Tuesday, where a prototype of the vehicle drew large crowds. Zhao said no one had yet been injured or hurt using the vehicle which, although described as a car, lacks wheels and is better described as a helicopter-style drone. He said the initial target market was people who were into “diving, surfing, off-roading and flying”.

Elon Musk last month showed off his version of a flying Tesla which uses high-powered blasts of gas to twist and flip in the air. Amid intense competition between the US and China over the development of electric vehicles and drone technology, Zhao said Musk’s prototype was “really hopping or jumping and not really flying”. The XPeng vehicle can cruise as high as 1km above the ground – well below an unpressurised light aircraft such as a Cessna.

“I’m looking forward to seeing a potential future generation that can actually fly,” he said, and agreed when asked if Musk’s showcase had the characteristics of a circus act.

However, the XPeng “flying car” also has limited scope. It will only be usable in approved park areas in China and by emergency services needing to reach inaccessible areas. It has a flight range of 30km (18.6 miles), although this will soon be doubled by increasing the battery’s energy density to 400 kilowatts per kilogram.

after newsletter promotion

Its emergence is part of a wider push by Beijing to develop what it calls the “low-altitude economy” – including drones and flying cars, starting with flying cargo, then people, and moving from rural areas to the cities. Zhao said his firm was one of about 20 in China working on flying vehicles.

“All cars in the future will grow wings and all transportation will move from two dimensions to three dimensions,” said Zhao, who claimed he had signed agreements with the United Arab Emirates and countries in south-east Asia to develop the flying car’s use, adding: “We aim to enter the European market as soon as possible.”

stories.title: MPs jostle for slice of £14.6m from axed leisure centre
stories.summary: Over £14m is available to be spent due to the cancellation of a new leisure centre in Bradford.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The proposed site of the Squire Lane leisure centre, formerly the location of the Springfield Children's Homes, is now locked up

Published 11 November 2026

Three Labour MPs in Bradford have found themselves scrapping it out for a share of £14.6m left over from a cancelled leisure centre project.

The Reform UK-led council axed the long-planned Squire Lane leisure centre project earlier this year, citing rising costs.

Shipley MP Anna Dixon had backed calls to use some of the money - which comes from a £20m government grant - to reopen Bingley Pool, while Bradford East MP Imran Hussain said last week he wanted a share to help turn a derelict building on his patch into a youth and community hub.

Meanwhile, Bradford West MP Naz Shah has recently said the cash should stay in the constituency it was meant for: "This money is something that I secured for Bradford West, and I'd like to keep it in Bradford West."

Naz Shah says the funding should stay in the constituency for which it was intended

The competing calls for the funding follow a recent row over whether Bradford could keep the grant at all .

Council leader Stephen Place had initially disputed Dixon's claim that the money was available for other projects, but later confirmed that the government would not claw it back . He said at the time that the council was not yet able to commit it to a particular scheme.

Shah has now told the BBC that the council leader had "absolutely assured" her Bradford West would be given "priority" when the money was allocated.

But she also said it was ultimately a matter for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) to decide on.

The BBC understands the money has to be spent by 2028.

Shipley MP Anna Dixon has previously said she wants officials to act on campaigners' wishes and use some of the government money to bring back Bingley Pool.

Asked whether the pot could be split between the three constituencies, hers and her two Labour colleagues', Shah pointed to the separate £20m allocated to Hussain's Bradford East constituency through the current government's Pride in Place programme.

She stressed it was every MP's own "choice and prerogative" to champion particular projects in their own constituencies with money earmarked specifically for those constituencies. "But the money that comes in to Bradford West, I'm very keen that it stays in Bradford West," she said.

Asked about her colleagues' efforts to secure some of the money , Shah said: "Is it the way I would have tried to get money for my constituency? No, it isn't."

But she said she had spoken to Dixon and understood why she was pressing for the swimming pool.

"That pool is something that she is passionate about, and rightfully so, because nobody would expect an MP not to be," Shah said.

Shah pointed to the Scotchman Road fields in Toller ward as one site on her patch that could benefit from investment and said there was further need across Bradford West, including in Clayton, Thornton, Manningham and Heaton.

"You could double and triple that [money], and I'd still find the need for it," she said.

'Serious injustice'

Bradford Independents Group councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed, who is chair of the cross-party Bradford West Area Committee, also backed Shah's call, saying: "Bradford West must not lose the investment it was promised."

He said the original Levelling Up grant was intended to tackle deprivation and health inequalities , and urged the council to commit the full £14.6m to alternative projects in Bradford West if ministers agreed.

"The cancellation of the original Squire Lane project does not cancel the needs of the people it was intended to serve," he said.

"I have no objection to Bingley residents campaigning for their swimming pool. They are entitled to make their case. But why should Bradford West lose out?"

The Heaton and Frizinghall councillor said not investing the money in Bradford West would "represent a serious injustice".

Bradford East MP Imran Hussain has urged the council to use Squire Lane funding to be invested into the Greenwood Centre, on his patch, which has been empty for many years and has become a target for vandalism and arson

The previous Conservative government had earmarked the £20m for the Squire Lane project through its Levelling Up programme.

But in July, the Reform-led executive decided to discontinue the project amid concerns about the council's financial position and rising costs. This was despite more than £5m of the original pot having already been spent on preparation and planning work.

The executive axed the project contrary to its own officers' recommendations, who had stressed in a report that the Bradford West area experiences "disproportionately high levels" of deprivation, physical inactivity, and poor physical and mental health.

Their report said Bradford West's lack of a publicly accessible swimming pool left "thousands of residents [facing] barriers in participating".

A Bradford Council spokesperson said the authority was "currently assessing options for alternative use of the Local Regeneration Funding previously allocated to the Squire Lane Leisure Centre project".

"Key to this is the need to ensure any projects are deliverable and can draw down on all required grant funds by end of March 2028," they added.

The BBC understands that a memorandum of understanding exists between Bradford Council and the MHCLG which sets out how Local Regeneration Funding is managed.

The authority would be expected to discuss any major changes with the MHCLG and while MPs would not have a formal role in that, they are considered to be significant stakeholders.

stories.title: Governments 'asleep at the wheel' over social care, says head of review
stories.summary: Baroness Casey criticises variability of services and fees charged to self-funders in England.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 11 November 2026

Successive governments have been "asleep at the wheel" on adult social care, says the head of the independent commission looking into the sector in England.

Baroness Louise Casey said care services for older people and adults with disabilities had been developed in a largely uncontrolled and unintended way, unlike the deliberate design of the NHS in 1948.

As a result, she suggested a postcode lottery had developed with different levels of services available depending on where people live.

And she also highlighted the fees that self-funders pay, saying they were much higher than councils were charged for people entitled to state support.

Baroness Casey said care services, such as home adaptations and personal care like helping people out of bed and with washing, were simply not valued enough.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said the NHS had become a "national hospital service: that was focussed on medical care".

'Heads in the sand'

And she said the failings identified by the recent Covid inquiry report into social care were testament to that.

Last month the inquiry published a report which said the care sector appeared to be " something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic, allowing Covid to spread like "wildfire" .

Baroness Casey, who will address a conference of social care leaders later on Wednesday, said the findings were "so awful" and "a national shame".

"Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel. We've got our heads in the sand."

Her final recommendations for services for older people and adults with disabilities, including care homes, will be published next summer.

It comes as her commission publishes research showing England is an international outlier for having no "clear system of stewardship" for social care, unlike countries such as France and Germany.

She said the market was dominated by private providers and said the regulator – the Care Quality Commission – as being a "spectator at the site of a car crash".

The research found:

Two people with the same condition having different experiences depending on where they live – different assessment processes, waits and levels of support

Those who paid for their own care – social care is means-tested – are charged on average 40% more than the councils pay for care they arrange

When Andy Burnham became prime minister, he said social care was one of his key priorities although the Casey commission was set up by the Starmer government.

"Together, we can build a new settlement for care," Baroness Casey said.

"One based on values I still believe this country shares – decency, contribution and a duty to care for our neighbours, our loved ones and ourselves."

stories.title: Acquitted 'China spy' tells BBC: I was fall guy for security services but also naive
stories.summary: Thousands of messages seen by BBC show how a Chinese official sought details of sensitive political matters.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page

Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested him

Published 11 November 2026

A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".

Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.

The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.

Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.

The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.

Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.

In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.

But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.

Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.

Chris Cash, left, and Chris Berry met in 2018 when they were teaching in China

With the government having previously said that Chinese spies were targeting UK officials across the political, defence and business sectors with increasingly sophisticated espionage operations, Cash believes his case was pursued as a warning to others.

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said he denied any wrongdoing and that he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media".

He said he had provided reports to a Chinese company, which he believed had clients seeking to develop trading links with the UK, and those reports contained no classified information and relied on public sources.

Cash returned to the UK in 2019, saying in his resignation message for his job in China that he felt "guilty sitting back and participating in a system that I am uncomfortable with".

He later became the director of a small policy group run by China-sceptic Conservative MPs in Westminster.

Meanwhile, Berry stayed in China writing reports for a large consultancy which, like many Chinese companies, has links to the government.

Inside the China Spy Case

The espionage row that rocked Westminster

Watch: Inside the China Spy Case on the BBC News YouTube channel , external

UK security services alleged that information from the men's messages, sent on the encrypted messaging app Signal between January 2022 and March 2023, had been passed to people linked to the Chinese state.

England and Wales' top prosecutor said the case had collapsed last autumn because government officials could not say China had been classed as an "enemy" at the time.

This prompted accusations of UK political interference to placate the Chinese government.

China has previously called the allegations of spying "pure fabrication and malicious slander".

'A psychological game of chess'

The most striking section of the messages handed to the BBC concerns Berry's account of his meeting in summer 2022 with a senior Chinese official who wanted to have "a more detailed co-operation".

In voice notes Berry describes how, beforehand, work colleagues had told him the official's interest had been piqued by reports Berry had written, which included details of the UK's foreign policy approach to China.

In the voice notes, Berry says he was initially aghast, but then decided: "I thought it would be interesting to go anyway… not really intending to do anything."

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Listen: Berry tells Cash about his invitation to meet a senior Chinese official

Berry tells Cash he was driven to a government-owned villa in a grand compound.

The experience "felt like a psychological game of chess" and "like a test", Berry says.

He kept his hands under the table as tea was served: "I didn't want it to be obvious if I was nervous. I tested to see if my hands were shaking first, then drank the tea."

Berry describes the senior Chinese official asking via an interpreter "about the situation in the UK at the moment, about the Tory leadership thing".

At that time, Boris Johnson had just resigned as the UK's prime minister, and a Conservative leadership battle was taking place, which Liz Truss would go on to win.

Berry says he jokingly tried to ask his host which candidate China wanted, but the interpreter did not translate his question.

"And then the main guy just shakes my hand like it's time to go," Berry tells Cash.

After receiving the voice notes, Cash replies via text the next day: "You, my friend, have just been elite captured" before adding: "You're in spy territory now".

In many media reports these particular messages, previously released in a government witness statement, have been presented as a smoking gun - evidence that Cash knew his friend was passing on information to the Chinese state.

But Cash insists it was a "tongue-in-cheek joke" because he knew his friend to be "a staunch critic of the Chinese Communist Party".

The next morning, he made a joke about Berry spying for the UK and getting in trouble with the Chinese authorities, he says. Cash texted: "Keep him sweet… We may have a use for you yet".

"I didn't believe he was knowingly spying on the UK through me," says Cash. "I trusted my friend… I wish I had seen the danger earlier, spotted it and cut off all contact."

'Bigger deal than I thought'

So who was the mystery official Berry had met?

"I found out who this guy is," Berry text-messaged Cash a few hours later. "Bigger deal than I thought."

Berry posted a link to the Wikipedia page of Cai Qi, who at the time was one of China's most influential politicians and is now, in effect, President Xi Jinping's chief of staff.

Berry identified Cai Qi (left) as the man he had met - a trusted aide of Chinese President Xi Jinping

Whether Berry correctly identified his host remains unclear. He has since disputed the suggestion that he met someone as senior as Cai Qi.

What is beyond dispute is that he believed he may have met someone highly placed within the Chinese political system.

For Chris Cash, this unusual encounter did not prompt alarm bells. Asked why not, Cash tells the BBC: "Because I didn't think anything of the meeting, really."

We ask Cash why his friend might have been asked to such a meeting. "Strange things happen in China... you know we would often brush shoulders with sort of quite senior members of the Chinese communist party," he tells us.

Challenged about whether he had read the Wikipedia link at the time, Cash says he had "skimmed it", adding that it described him as a judge and a provincial-level official. "I just thought it was a weird meeting with a guy who'd taken an interest," he says.

Six months later, Berry said in text messages that "off the record" he had it "on pretty good authority" that China was considering dropping sanctions against Tom Tugendhat, one of the Conservative MPs in the China Research Group, where Cash worked.

Berry wrote that this would happen as long as the West "continued to show signals that they are willing to work together".

The Chinese believed it would be "extremely embarrassing" if Tugendhat became prime minister or foreign secretary while under Chinese sanctions, Berry said.

At the time of the meeting in summer 2022, China-sceptic Tugendhat was seen as a possible contender to succeed Boris Johnson, or become UK foreign secretary.

He was actually appointed as security minister by Liz Truss, and Beijing lifted sanctions on him in January 2026.

Was Cash concerned that Berry appeared to be passing information to him about Chinese foreign policy?

Cash says he assumed Berry had heard this "through the grapevine at his company" which was doing business with the UK.

He says he never doubted his friend's trustworthiness, to the extent he even named Berry as a reference on his application for a security pass for the Palace of Westminster.

The pass was granted and, a fortnight before their arrests in early 2023, Cash invited Berry to Parliament for lunch.

It was to be their final face-to-face conversation.

'Complete shock'

Cash was in bed at quarter to six on a March morning when he was woken by car doors being shut, he says. Within seconds, four UK counter-terrorism officers had barged into his bedroom at his parents' home in Edinburgh.

"They told me to sit up and not touch anything and then said I was under arrest for breaching the Official Secrets Act," Cash says.

"I was in complete shock… quivering... My mum was hysterical."

Cash says the officers dressed him in dirty clothes he had worn that weekend, handcuffed him and marched him down to an unmarked police car. He was later driven to London.

Chris Berry was also arrested the same day.

It remains unclear how, when and why British security services became interested in the exchanges between the two friends.

But they are likely to have found out far more about their relationship when Berry was stopped and questioned by counter-terror officers at Heathrow Airport.

His laptop and phone were taken - this may have enabled his Signal chats to be downloaded.

Berry later messaged Cash about it.

Cash says he had not been alarmed by this: "I thought it was just standard... for a guy who'd been in China."

As the investigation progressed, it became clear the authorities believed Cash and Berry had been involved in an informal, but dangerous, exchange of information that was "prejudicial to the safety and interests of the UK".

The allegations were based on 6,273 messages between the pair - the same ones Cash has now shared with the BBC. Cash's solicitor has told the BBC they are genuine.

They cover a period when Cash had joined the China Research Group (CRG), founded by Tugendhat and fellow Tory MP Alicia Kearns, and when Berry was working for a Chinese company called Strong, where part of his work involved writing political and economic reports for clients.

According to court documents, Berry was said to have compiled 34 reports for a man linked to the Chinese state spy agency, relaying information passed on to him by Cash. Strong did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

The CRG's office was across the Thames from Westminster, but Cash regularly had meetings in Parliament. Cash did not have government security clearance and there is no evidence he had access to classified documents.

Despite being thousands of miles apart, the two friends remained in close contact, often messaging daily.

The messages reviewed by the BBC show them discussing topics including sanctions on China, the tech company Huawei, human rights, Hong Kong, Taiwan and British foreign policy.

Cash says he used the Signal app for almost all his contacts with people in China - "more for their protection" - as he says discussing the government "could land someone… in trouble". He and Berry did not use the app's "disappearing messages" function.

Much of the information they discussed was publicly available, says Cash - who has given the BBC a detailed spreadsheet with links and references in an attempt to prove it.

But sometimes he did share with Berry his impressions from meetings and private discussions in Westminster. On 12 occasions in the messages, he labelled information "off the record" or "very off the record" before passing it on.

Cash says this was "just me excitedly sharing things that I was doing with him at work".

One message recounted views allegedly expressed in private by Britain's then-ambassador to China, Dame Caroline Wilson, during a discussion with the CRG about its work on China's influence on UK universities.

Cash also messaged Berry sharing unverified rumours about the sex lives of two UK cabinet ministers. There is no evidence Berry passed this to his Chinese colleagues.

Cash says he regarded such exchanges as routine political discussion. "We weren't working with classified information," he says.

Acquitted and 'traduced'

Cash was told by his solicitor the police investigation would blow over after six months and he would soon be able to return to normal life.

But in September 2023 - six months after the arrests - the case became public when the Sunday Times broke the story of an unnamed "spy" who had been arrested in Parliament.

Cash recalls travelling on a train while, around him, fellow passengers read the newspaper's front page story: "Commons 'Chinese spy' arrested". He says: "I wanted the world to eat me up."

Within 24 hours he was named and pictured in the press, and both men were later charged with espionage.

In September the following year, just weeks before their trial was due to begin, Cash received an unexpected call from his solicitor.

"Are you sitting down?" he asked Cash. "They've dropped all the charges."

His lawyers requested a court hearing for the prosecution to formally acknowledge that they would offer no evidence, but at the Old Bailey the newly-innocent Cash struggled to find anyone interested in his story.

Cash's life has changed almost beyond recognition, he says, but he is positive about the future

At every previous court appearance he had been mobbed, but the press had not been informed about this hearing.

Eventually his team found a lone BBC journalist. "I said my piece outside the Old Bailey. And that was a real high point. I felt that I could start to move on with my life."

It wouldn't be that simple.

Across the city, House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle was seething. "It is this Parliament that has been spied on," he declared. "It is MPs' offices that have been infiltrated."

There would be days of political debate and a raucous prime minister's questions where Tory leader Kemi Badenoch would claim: "This all stinks of a cover-up."

"I'd been acquitted by law, but then I was traduced in Parliament," Cash says. "It was almost like I was convicted in the court of public opinion again, by people who I had worked with and trusted and that felt horrible."

Today Cash's life is almost unrecognisable. He has lost his dream job, his relationship, and his closest friend from university.

"We talked about being each other's best men," Cash says. Instead, when the friend got married last year, Cash was not even invited.

He is also no longer in contact with Berry.

"I've been applying for basic admin jobs and having trouble recently," Cash says.

"I'm angry and upset with how everything played out, and I do feel let down."

But when asked, Cash stops short of saying he feels Berry betrayed him. Does he think his friend was spying for the Chinese government?

"He would have to have his time in court to defend himself," Cash answers. "I think it'd be wrong of me to speculate and hypocritical given the speculation that I've been subject to. But we're no longer friends."

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said his reports "concerned economic and commercial issues widely discussed in the UK at the time and drew on information freely in the public domain".

Like his former friend, Chris Cash is innocent in the eyes of the law, but his reputation has undoubtedly been trashed.

Many in Parliament still think they were spies. And with more of the messages between these former friends now revealed, the debate over their actions could be reignited.

"It was a gruelling ordeal," Cash says. "But I'm a fundamentally positive person… I'm positive about what the future holds."
